  `.by_id(`, `get::<Collider>`, `.aabb_min`, `.aabb_max`, `PhysicsWorld::collider`/`colliders`/`by_id` or `&Collider` type (a query or
  an argument: a field is no entity with a `Collider`) in `crates/*/src` outside `shards_motion/src/physics/` that is not in
  `tests/readers.allow` with its reason, a row for each time a file has the line, and on a row that matches no line.
- A field is not saved and has no `AiId` (as level geometry, the region that spawned it spawns it again); the snapshot check
  `static_colliders` hashes every field (size, cell, origin, cast mode, bits and layers), and a world without one hashes as before. The
  engine rule `voxel.body_in_solid` (`BODY_IN_SOLID`, `body_in_solid`) names a character whose capsule centre is in a solid cell of a
  field it collides with, except on the tick something other than the controller placed it (`MotionState::placed`). It is **on by
  default**, an ordinary engine rule: it was offered off by default (mantle and sloped-step ticks might graze a cell) until fuzz runs on
  voxel terrain passed (the voxel design, 6.4), and 50 runs of `shards fuzz --steps 600` on the sandbox's voxel arena with it on (20
  without chaos, 20 with `--chaos 0.02`, 10 more with `--chaos 0.02 --steer`) stopped on nothing. `add_opt_in_engine_invariant` stays for the
  next such rule: it registers an engine rule only when `EngineConfig::opt_in_invariants` names it, and `--engine-invariant NAME` names
  one (a name the build does not offer is refused, and the flag does not go with `--no-engine-invariants`); none is offered today.
- Checked by `crates/shards_motion/tests/motion/seams.rs`: each scenario runs in four worlds, one cuboid collider per cell, the merged
  boxes as colliders, the field, and the field with the merge off (stand on seams, an edge and a corner; one-cell walls; mixed
  heights; steps of 0.3, 0.5 and 1 m; a mantle; tunnels, with the probe, the hooks and `clearance` at 1350 spots in and around
  them against the merged boxes; landing on a seam; a checkerboard diagonal; 16 bodies on rolling hills), and each says what must have
  happened (standing bodies stay put on the ground on every tick, sliders stay on their side of the wall, the checkerboard is crossed
  and climbed). The field with the merge off equals the cells to the bit on every tick; with the merge on, the scripted scenarios stay
  within 3e-6 m and 2.4e-4 m/s of the cells with the same modes. Ground normals are not compared: at a seam or an edge GJK's normal off
  a cell is noise (up to 56° on the checkerboard, positions equal). On the hills (16 bodies, 600 ticks; 40 seeds walked by hand with
  `SEAMS_SEEDS=1..=40`, three in the test), one step from the same state stays within 1e-4 m (at most 7e-5 m) but for two steps on
  seed 6 that went another way (a mantle taken in the field, a step in the cells), and on both the merged boxes as colliders went the
  field's way; the merged boxes take another step than the cells on 279 body-ticks of the 40 seeds. A free-running walk amplifies
  rounding at corners as any chaotic system does (a step-up decided on an edge ride): the merged field and the cells part by more than
  1e-4 m on 33 of the 40 seeds, first at tick 115 to 572 (on seed 7, 10 of 16 bodies from tick 147, one by 32 cm), and the test holds the
  first 100 ticks. The merged boxes as colliders part for more bodies (365 against the field's 117) and first or alone on 39 of the 40
  seeds. With the merge off the field never parts from the cells. The voxel design's criterion (section 15: within 1e-4 m over the free
  walk) is not met as written; that is the lead's call (the design's risk 10).
  `field_timing` (`#[ignore]`, release; the least of seven samples, the medians within 3 %): on 64 m of 0.5 m-cell hills the ground cast
  takes 8.2 µs with the merge, 16.8 µs without and 15.3 µs as column boxes; rays 0.16–0.75 µs (1.5–1.8 times faster than the boxes, the
  sight ray 16 times), `overlaps` 6.7 times faster; the walk cast (0.1 m) and `closer_than` are slower than the boxes, 5.2 against
  4.8 µs and 1.54 against 1.33 µs.

**Why parry3d and not avian3d.** The spec named avian3d as a candidate and required checking Bevy 0.20 support before taking a third-party crate. Checked against the crates.io index (13–14 October 2026): avian3d 0.7.0 requires Bevy 0.19, and Bevy is pinned
to 0.20.0 (the same goes for bevy_enhanced_input 0.26.0 and lightyear 0.30.1). A kinematic controller needs collision queries, not dynamics, so `parry3d =0.31.1` was taken (dimforge geometry, it does not depend on Bevy; avian is built on it too).
It is pinned, lives inside `shards_motion`, and stays out of the public API: the API speaks glam (`Vec3`, `Quat`) and its own
`Shape`. It can go back to avian3d once it supports Bevy 0.20, without touching the game. By the same check, the input map is its own, not
`bevy_enhanced_input`.

**Controller.** `CharacterController { params: "id" }` is a capsule that only it moves (actions such as a roll hand their displacement to it, and a wall stops a lunge). Modes: ground (walking, running, sprinting, slopes up to `max_slope_deg`,
steps up to `step_height`, sticking down on stairs), air (gravity, control in the air, a jump with "coyote time" and a buffer), glider (slow fall, updrafts), water (swimming on the surface, getting out over shallows or by a jump), climbing onto a ledge
up to `mantle_height` along a path checked in advance. Characters do not block each other as they pass: after everyone has moved, in id order, the capsules are pushed apart. A fall from height is the event `Landed {
fall_height }`, plus `Jumped`, `Mantled`, `ModeChanged`. A body whose `locomotion` gives a `crouch_height` can crouch (F2, "Crouching (F2)"): `Crouched`, `Stood`. The `Transform` position is the feet; writing to it from outside (`teleport`, respawn) places the character again, with no speed and no fall.

**Ground laid in the middle of play (R2).** The controller stands on, and is stopped by, every `WORLD` collider that is not a
volume, `Body::Static` and `Body::Kinematic` alike. A plain kinematic collider does not carry what stands on it: a body on one that
moves is left behind (a mover does carry it: see "Movers (F6)" below). So a game makes temporary ground (a toppled giant to walk along to its core)
with no engine code. While the body lies still, the game spawns static colliders shaped to the lying pose; when it rises, the
game despawns them. The rules:

- *From the simulation.* Lay and lift them in `FixedUpdate` in a `SimSet`, on every machine that simulates. `sync_physics` keeps
  `PhysicsWorld` in step with the ECS: a collider spawned during a tick is ground from the next tick, and a despawn takes it out at
  once. A replay runs the same code, so the ground comes and goes on the same ticks.
- *With an `AiId`.* Give each collider `AiKind`, so it gets an `AiId`. Then a snapshot saves it and brings it back (`Collider`,
  `Body`, `ColliderId` and `Transform` are reflected), and co-op sends it to the clients, whose prediction stands on it too.
  Without an `AiId` it counts as level geometry, which a snapshot does not hold: the `static_colliders` check compares the
  colliders without an `AiId` and refuses a load into a game where they differ (one that has not laid the same collider, with
  the same id and pose, before loading), and a client never gets it.
- *Navigation.* The navmesh cuts out a laid collider at its next refresh but bakes no walkable surface on top of it (see
  "Navigation and NPCs (E6)"). Each tick's NPC routing refreshes it first; `move_to path=true` and `path_to` read it as it
  stands, so a route they plan before that refresh (on the tick the ground is laid) can still cross it. After it, a route never
  leads onto laid ground. A plain move walks onto it, and a ledge up to `mantle_height` is climbed.
- *Foliage.* The scatter does not clear the grass under a collider laid after the layout (see "What counts as ground and what
  as solid" in "Foliage and small objects (E10.2)"). That rule belongs to the scatter, not to the controller.

Tests:

- `shards_motion` `tests/motion/ground.rs`: a slab laid from a system, static or kinematic, is landed on and walked along, and
  is climbed like any ledge; when it goes, the body falls back to the floor. A kinematic slab that slides away
  leaves the body where it stood.
- The sandbox's `snapshots.rs` and `net.rs`: the same slab with `AiKind` survives a load and reaches a client, and its removal
  reaches both.

**Movers (F6): doors, lifts, platforms.** A mover is an entity with `Mover { def }` that goes through the keys of a `mover`
definition (content kind `mover`, `*.mover.ron`), carries the characters that stand on it and pushes the ones in its way.
A level node with `mover=<id>` makes one (its children in the file move with it, as its `MoverPart`s, and its picture follows
it: the node in the level's scene with the same whole path below the scene's own root); so does a prefab or a spawn with the `Mover` component and a `Collider`.

```ron
// assets/content/world/movers.mover.ron
{
    "lift": (keys: [(), (at: (0.0, 4.0, 0.0))], speed: 1.2),
    "gate": (keys: [(), (at: (-3.0, 0.0, 0.0))], speed: 1.5, blocked: Reverse),
    "crusher": (keys: [(), (at: (0.0, -2.6, 0.0))], speed: 1.0, blocked: Crush(damage: 10.0)),
    "turntable": (keys: [(), (turn: (0.0, 360.0, 0.0), time: 8.0)], loop: Cycle),
}
```

- *Keys* (2 to 64) are poses relative to where the mover was placed, in its frame (a gate turned in the level slides along its
  own axis): `at` (metres), `turn` (degrees about X, Y, Z), `time` (seconds from the key before; without it the way takes its
  length over `speed` m/s or its turn over `turn_speed` °/s, whichever is slower), `wait` (seconds it rests there; the definition's
  `wait` by default). It starts at key 0.
- *`loop`*: `Off` (by default: it goes only where it is sent, and stops at that key), `PingPong` (up the keys and back, resting
  `wait` at each end), `Cycle` (up the keys, then from the last straight on to key 0, which must be the same pose).
- *`blocked`*, when a body is in its way and cannot be pushed out (against a wall, pinned under it): `Stop` (by default: it waits
  where it is and goes on once the body has gone), `Reverse` (it turns back to the key it came from), `Crush(damage, every)` (it
  holds, and the body takes `damage` when the hold begins and every `every` seconds, 1 by default, while it lasts).
- The content check names the file and the field (`content/world/movers.mover.ron: lift: keys[1]: the way from key 0 takes no
  time; it moves 4.00 m: give the mover a speed`, `loop: Cycle goes from the last key back to key 0 at once, so keys[1] must be
  where key 0 is`, `blocked: Crush damage must be above 0`, and a way shorter than `MIN_WAY`, 0.01 s: `keys[1]: the way from key 0 takes 0.001 s, under
  the shortest a way may take (0.01 s)`; a step then passes a bounded number of keys, and a long one runs all of its time as short
  ones would), and a level node that names a mover content does not have (``node `Lifts/Lift`: `mover`:
  no mover definition `lfit` (did you mean `lift`?); movers: lift, slide``). Movers do not nest.

*The tick.* `MoverSystems::Step` runs in `SimSet::Move` before the controller. Each character on the ground is asked what it
stands on (the controller's ground probe). Then each mover, in `AiId` order, runs its state on and puts its colliders where it
would stand. A body that stood on it is carried by the mover's motion this tick: its translation, and for a turning mover the
turn about the mover's pivot, with the body's yaw turned along. A body it now sinks into (a closing door, a lift from below) is
pushed out the shortest way, sliding against the world. A body that cannot be pushed out blocks the step: the mover stays where
it was, and its `blocked` rule acts. Otherwise the pose, the bodies and the state are written. A body keeps only its own velocity:
stepping or jumping off a mover, it takes none of the mover's along. Movers push characters only (players and NPCs); they pass
through static geometry, other movers and props. A plain kinematic collider without `Mover` still carries and pushes nothing (R2).

*Its bodies.* At rest a mover's colliders are `Body::Static`, so a closed door is cut out of the navmesh at its next refresh like
any laid solid (and an open one where it rests); while it moves they are `Body::Kinematic`, which the navmesh leaves out. NPCs walk
around a closed door and through an open one. They do not ride lifts: a lift as a navigation link is later work.

*API.* `mover_go(world, mover, key)` sends a mover to a key and returns a `MoverInfo`; it is an `Err` with the reason on a machine
that does not simulate, for what is no mover, and for a key the definition lacks (``no key 4: `lift` has keys 0..=1``).
`mover_state(world, mover)` reads one: key, next key, progress, goal, velocity, turn rate, wait, hold, the seconds to the goal.
Events: `MoverStarted { mover, from, to }`, `MoverArrived { mover, key }`, `MoverBlocked { mover, body, damage }`. A crushing
mover's `MoverBlocked` carries its damage, and the action module deals it through `deal_damage` on the machine that simulates:
no credit (the crusher is the world, not a fighter), and not scaled by the rules. The state (`MoverState` on the mover) is in
snapshots, the replay hash and co-op; the engine rule `motion.mover_sane` holds it to its definition.

*For an agent.* `observe` describes a mover as `e14 Mover "Lift"  key 0→1, moving up 1.2m/s` (or `at key 1`; then `, turning 45°/s`,
`, leaves in 0.5s`, `, to key 2` when it goes on past the next key, `, held 1.0s`). The dev tool `mover_go id=eN key=K` (or `name=Lift`; a typo gets ``no mover named `lfit`
(did you mean `Lift`?); movers: e14 Lift, e15 Gate``) answers `ok: e14 Lift goes to key 1 (3.3s)`. The condition
`step --until named:mover_arrived` holds on the tick a mover stops at a key; a looping mover with no `wait` never stops, so it never
arrives. The journal says when a mover that goes only where it is sent leaves and arrives (`e14 Lift leaves key 0 for key 1`,
`e14 Lift at key 1`) and what holds it (`e16 Crusher crushes e5 Player (10)`, `e15 Gate held by e5 Player`); a looping mover's
rounds stay out of it.

*Co-op.* The host moves movers. A client never writes their state, which is replicated (the desync hash compares it). A client
predicts its own body on a mover against the mover where it will be at the predicted tick (`MoverSystems::Predict`, in
`NetSet::Predict` before the predicted move): it runs the replicated state on by the ticks between the host's tick and its own (at
most two seconds' worth), puts the mover's colliders there in its own physics world only, and carries and pushes its own body as
the host does. The host stays authoritative, and the usual correction mends what the client did not know yet. That is a mover's
start: a call reaches the host at a tick the client does not predict, so for about a round trip the client has its body standing
still. In the sandbox's test, with 150 ms each way, the error peaks under 0.5 m and the correction takes it back, with no snap and no
desync. It is also a block the client did not foresee. A level mover's picture on a client follows the host's poses as they come
(it is not blended between ticks as on a machine that simulates), so a predicted body on it can look a little off until the next
state.

Tests: `shards_motion` `tests/motion/movers.rs` (a body rides a lift up and down and keeps its feet; a jump on a rising lift; a
turntable carries a body and turns it; a door pushes a body; `Stop`, `Reverse` and `Crush`; ping-pong and cycle; a snapshot taken
mid-ride plays on the same; the describer, the tool, the condition; bad definitions); `shards_level` `tests/level/movers.rs` (a node
and its children move together, in the frame they were put in; a snapshot keeps the parts; an unknown and a nested mover;
`level_despawn`; the picture follows, with `render`, and two movers whose paths end alike, `A/Mover` and `B/A/Mover`, each
find their own node); `shards_action` `tests/combat/crush.rs`; `shards_npc` `tests/npc/navmesh.rs`
(a closed door is carved, an open one where it rests); the sandbox's `movers.rs` (the room's file, each mover's picture on its own node of the scene Bevy
loads, its scenario on a fresh game leaving nothing behind, a client riding a lift the host moves), `engine_rules.rs` (`motion.mover_sane` fires), the scenario
`movers.scenario` and its reference replay `movers.json`.

**Parameters are content.** Content kind `locomotion`, a map from id to numbers; missing fields take default values, a typo is an error with its line.
They are read every tick, so an edit to the file changes the next step.

```ron
// assets/content/characters.locomotion.ron
{ "hero": (radius: 0.4, height: 1.8, walk_speed: 2.0, run_speed: 5.5, sprint_speed: 8.0, jump_height: 1.3) }
```

The other fields (`acceleration`, `deceleration`, `snap_distance`, `gravity`, `coyote_time`, `jump_buffer`, `air_control`,
`terminal_speed`, `mantle_height`, `mantle_time`, `swim_depth`, `float_depth`, `swim_speed`, `glide_fall_speed`,
`glide_speed`, `glide_accel`, `turn_speed_deg`) are described in `shards_motion::CharacterParams`.

**Locomotion modifiers (port gap G7, motion half).** `MoveModifiers` is a component every `CharacterController` gets. It is *derived and
stateless*: each tick it is put back to neutral, then the sources add what they want, so nothing is remembered, and the component is
in no snapshot and no replay (the sources are). It holds: `factor` (multiplies every voluntary speed, a swim too), `ground_factor`
(ground and air only: combat pace, wading), `cap` (no ground speed above it, a sprint included), `unsprinted_cap` (a walk or run only: a
lock-on's pace, which a sprint passes), `no_sprint`, `rooted`, `sprint_cost` (a multiplier, 0 is a free sprint), `wade` (the wading factor alone, also inside `ground_factor`), `stance` (a stance's own top
speed) and `acceleration` / `deceleration` (rate overrides). Sources use `slow`, `slow_on_ground`, `wade_by`, `cap_at`, `cap_unsprinted_at`, `forbid_sprint`, `root`, `scale_sprint_cost`, `stance_speed`,
`accelerate_at`, `decelerate_at`: factors multiply, caps take the lowest, a stance takes the lowest top speed, the last rate wins.

Order inside `SimSet::Input` (after the orders, before the NPC brains), so every reader sees this tick's value:
`ModifierSystems::Reset` → `Contribute` (`Wade`, then `Statuses`, then the game's systems, which must be ordered among themselves:
`.in_set(ModifierSystems::Contribute).after(ModifierSystems::Statuses)`). A client's own body does the same in `NetSet::Predict`
(`PredictReset`, `PredictWade`, `PredictStatuses`, `PredictContribute`); a game adds its source to both. A source that reads an
action sees last tick's end state.

The controller composes for walking and air control: `speed = min(min(ground_speed, cap), unsprinted_cap unless sprinting) * factor *
ground_factor` (with `caps_scale_with_input` the caps are ratios of the full-input speed), or, under a `stance`, `top * stick * wade` (no `factor`, no `ground_factor`, no sprint); a swim is `swim_speed` (or `swim_fast_speed`) `* factor`; a root zeroes voluntary motion exactly like an action's
`locked` (no walking, jumping, gliding, climbing; gravity and `external` still apply). All neutral takes the plain path (replays
are unchanged). The NPC route follower (`top` speed), the animation picker (`BodyStatus::pace`: a slowed run still plays the run clip,
slower), the action machine and `update_fighters` (sprint cost) read the same component.

*Statuses.* `StatusDef` has `speed_factor`, `speed_cap` and `root` (all optional); an active status adds them (`shards_action::
statuses_to_modifiers`). *Wading* is in the params: `wade_min_depth`, `wade_full_depth`, `wade_factor` (1: off); the walk slows in a straight
line with the depth of water over the feet, and a swimmer does not wade.

*Composing a typical action-game pace* (`speed = base * pace * stat * wade * stick`, base 6.7 sprinting, else 4.5 locked on, else 5.0; a guard walks at `3.0 * wade * stick`, a
drinking walk at `2.5 * wade`; none of the stances is scaled by the stat slow or the pace): content `walk_speed` 2.5, `run_speed` 5.0 (so the stick maps linearly),
`sprint_speed` 6.7 with `sprint_scales_with_input`, `caps_scale_with_input`, `wade_*`; game sources: combat `slow_on_ground(0.85)` (not while guarding
or swimming), lock-on `cap_unsprinted_at(4.5)` (a ratio of the full-input speed with `caps_scale_with_input`, so a 0.7 stick walks at `4.5 * 0.7`), guard `stance_speed(3.0, true)` (the status slow and the pace do
not touch it, wading does, a sprint does nothing), a drinking walk `stance_speed(2.5, false)`, out of combat `scale_sprint_cost(0.0)` (a free sprint still holds the stamina
regeneration back), chill `speed_factor: 0.75`. The caps come before the factors, so a locked-on walk is `4.5 * 0.85`.

*Which factors reach which state.* The table is what a game that must match an exact rulebook reads off its own source, then expresses with the options:

| state | speed is | options |
|---|---|---|
| free walk or run | `base * pace * stat * wade * stick` | `factor` (stat), `ground_factor` (pace, wade), `walk_speed`/`run_speed` |
| sprint | `sprint * pace * stat * wade * stick` | `sprint_scales_with_input` (else full speed above half a stick) |
| locked on | like a walk, with a lower top speed | `cap_unsprinted_at`, `caps_scale_with_input` |
| guard, drinking walk | `top * wade [* stick]` only | `stance_speed(top, by_input)`, `accelerate_at`/`decelerate_at` |
| swim | `swim * stat * stick` (no pace, no wade, no cap) | `factor` only |
| dodge, a push | fixed | `external` |

*Acceleration.* By default the speed steps along the straight line to the target, at `acceleration` when the target is at least as fast as the body and `deceleration` otherwise, and the air
keeps its horizontal speed with no input. Options, all off by default: `axis_stepping` (x and z each step toward their own target, as some action games do),
`brake_only_without_input` (`deceleration` only with no input; with input `acceleration` always, also toward a slower target), `air_deceleration` (braking in the air with no
input; `air_control` 1 makes the speed-up there the full `acceleration`), and per-stance rates from a source: `MoveModifiers::accelerate_at` / `decelerate_at` replace the params
for that tick (ground and air, also the air braking); the last writer wins, so order the sources.

That is the `Step` model, the default. The `accel` option replaces it on the ground and in the air with the model of *Quake* and *Half-Life* (friction, and a push limited by the speed already projected on the wished direction): see "Air movement in the style of Half-Life (F7)" below.

*Sprint in the air.* The sprint flag (the speed and the stamina drain) is decided on the ground and in the water. With `sprint_in_air` the air decides it every tick as well, by the same
rule: pressing sprint in the air starts the sprint and letting go ends it on that tick (the take-off value no longer lasts the whole jump), and a glide is no sprint. The host and the client's
prediction both read the flag from `MotionState`, so they agree. Off by default.

*Statuses.* A body that takes a status but is not slowed by it (a large enemy that gets a chill buildup and its other effects but keeps its speed) carries the marker
`NoStatusSlow`: the `speed_factor` and `speed_cap` of its statuses are skipped, a `root` is not. `StatusResist` is for a body that should not take the status at all. A game can also leave `speed_factor`
unset and contribute the slow itself from a `Contribute` system that reads the statuses and the kind of the body.

*Wading depth.* The depth wading reads is `surface - feet + wade_depth_offset` (never below 0), for a game that measures submersion at a reference point under the soles: the value
to use is the gap from that point to the floor of a standing body, that is its distance below the capsule bottom plus `skin_width` (a point 0.1 m under the capsule bottom with
the default skin is `0.12`). `wade_in_air` lets the water over the feet slow an airborne body too (a glide is not slowed: modifiers do not scale it). A reference point fixed under the capsule bottom is a skin closer to the feet in the air than for a standing body (the feet
rest a skin above the floor only on the ground), so `wade_air_depth_offset` (default: the standing `wade_depth_offset`) sets the airborne value, `wade_depth_offset - skin_width` for such a point. `move_info` shows `wade_depth` (the depth used), `wade_factor`, `wade_depth_offset`, `wade_air_depth_offset` and `climb_out_reach`, and no wading outside the modes
that wade. Wading and the offset affect only the speed, not floating, swimming or landing.

*Stamina after a dry sprint.* `CombatTuning::sprint_resume` (land) and `CharacterParams::swim_fast_resume` (fast swim) are a `SprintResume`: `OnRelease` (the default: the button must be let
go, then any stamina is enough) or `Fraction(f)` (back once the stamina is at least `f` of its maximum, button held or not; letting go does not open it). `Fraction(0.25)` is a lock that
opens at a quarter; `Fraction(0)` has no lock at all: the sprint stops at an empty bar and goes on as soon as there is any stamina. A lock set by one rule is consulted only by a rule that has a lock,
so a fast swim lock survives a walk on land, and a dry land sprint under `Fraction(0)` does not lock the next swim. The bar counts as empty at `<= 0.0001`, not exactly 0.

*Limits to know:* a status slow also applies under a cap (a game exempts a state by not adding the factor, or with a stance); caps do not apply to a swim.

*Controller options for an exact rulebook (C4).* Each is content, off by default and unserialized when off, so content hashes and the reference replays do not change.

- *Turning speed by who asks.* `turn_speed_deg` is the free rate. `locked_turn_speed_deg` (0: the free rate) applies while the input names a facing: a lock-on target, an aim point, or a running action's own facing (`LocomotionInput::face`). An action can set its own rate with `ActionDef::turn_speed_deg` (a raised guard); it reaches the controller through `MoveModifiers::turn_speed_deg` (`turn_at(deg)`, the lowest source wins), filled by `actions_to_modifiers` from the action the last tick left, so the rate takes hold one tick after the action starts (a client's own body reads the action it shows, its `PredictedAction`, and none while it shows none, as the prediction moves it). A swimmer keeps `swim_turn_speed_deg`. The order is: swim (in water, when set), then a stance's rate, then the locked rate, then the free one. These are rates of the body only: an action's `turn` spans (B2a, "Turning" under the action timeline) turn the run's own facing, where its hits, guard and displacement point, and the controller turns the body toward that facing once a tick at the rate above. On a tick where both apply, each bounds its own: the run turns at the spans' rate, the body follows no faster than its rate, and nothing turns the body twice. An action with turn spans (and `face: Run`) names a facing on every tick, so its body follows at the locked rate when that is set; a rate below the spans' leaves the body behind its swing. `turn_toward_input` makes the body turn toward the movement input while there is one, not toward its velocity, so a body pressed against a wall (velocity held at 0) still turns to face it; with no input it turns toward its velocity as before. `move_info` shows `turn_free_deg`, `turn_locked_deg`, `turn_swim_deg`, `turn_toward_input` and the stance's `turn_speed_deg`.
- *Water entry, in closed form.* `entry_max_speed` (m/s, 0: no brake) scales the horizontal velocity down to that speed once, in the tick the water takes the body (a run or a jump into a pool). `buoyancy_omega` (1/s, 0: the first-order drift to the float line and an entry fall held to `swim_speed`, as before) replaces the drift by a critically damped spring toward the float line, stepped by its exact solution `x(dt) = (x0 + (v0 + w x0) dt) e^(-w dt)`, `v(dt) = (v0 - w (v0 + w x0) dt) e^(-w dt)` through `ops::exp`: no step-by-step integration, so the plunge does not depend on the tick rate. With the spring the entry fall is not held to the swim speed, so a dive plunges past the float line and rises back to it; `water_max_vertical_speed` (0: `swim_speed`, so set it above `swim_speed` to let a dive plunge; with only `buoyancy_omega` the fall is still held to `swim_speed`) bounds the speed and the travel of a tick, and `water_fall_drag` slows a fall in the water as `exp(-drag t)`. Entering the water already takes the body out of the air and the ground (`MotionMode::Water`), so there is nothing to force.
- *Climb-out.* `climb_out_min_facing` (a dot product, 0.5 is within 60 degrees; `None`: no test) needs the body to face the ledge (the direction into the wall, opposite its normal) for both the push and the jump; a land mantle is never tested. A swimmer that does not face the ledge does not climb and keeps swimming, in control; there is no search to the sides (set `turn_toward_input` so that pressing against a ledge turns the body to it). `climb_out_time` (`None`: `mantle_time`) is the length of a climb that starts in the water.
- *Crawl lock.* The fast swim's lock that ends at a fraction of the bar with no sprint input is `swim_fast_resume: Fraction(0.25)` (see "Stamina after a dry sprint"); the lock arms when the crawl runs the bar dry and opens by itself once the bar is at a quarter, whether or not the button is held, so no emulation of a check that runs only while crawling is needed.

Tests: `crates/shards_motion/tests/motion/controller_parity.rs`, the unit tests of the spring in `locomotion.rs`, and `crates/sandbox/scenarios/player_controller_parity.scenario` (the scenario adds and removes its own definitions with `content_apply`).

*Swimming.* `swim_fast_speed` (a sprint in water) costs `swim_fast_drain` stamina per second, always (the sprint cost multiplier does not
apply) and ends at no stamina or `no_sprint`; `swim_acceleration`, `swim_deceleration`, `swim_turn_speed_deg` (0: the ground's numbers).
Climbing out of water has two tiers. With `climb_out_auto_height` (above the water surface), pushing against a ledge climbs it by itself up to that height. A jump climbs up to `climb_out_max_height`
**above the surface** when that is set (the probe reaches that high and the controller, the `jump` tool, `clearance` and the planner agree through `CharacterParams::can_jump_out`), so a game whose ledge window is
"up to 1.3 m over the water" sets it without raising `mantle_height` (which would also raise the climb on land); without it the jump uses `mantle_height` above the feet, that is `mantle_height - float_depth`
over the surface. `climb_out_reach` (default 0.3 m) is how far in front of the body the ledge face may be for the water climb-out: the controller's probe and the `jump` tool both read
`CharacterParams::climb_reach()`, and a larger value also closes the gap to the wall before the step over, so a swimmer half a meter off a deck climbs out. Not covered: a search to the sides of the swimmer (the facing test is `climb_out_min_facing`, see C4 below). Pushing never climbs higher than `climb_out_auto_height` (plus the 1 mm of float slack `mantle_height` has too, so a ledge exactly at the height climbs). *Landing:* `Landed` has `tier` (how many of `landing_tiers` the impact speed reached) and `jumped`
(`landing_drop_tiers` for a fall that did not follow a jump; the controller marks a jump's flight with `JumpedFlight` only when tiers are set, so tiers added by hot reload while a character is airborne apply from its next jump);
`landing_wade_limit` drops the event where the water over the feet is deeper. The journal says `e5 landed from 0.4m at 4.9m/s, tier 1 (jump)`.
Coyote time is `coyote_time` (0.12 s by default).

For the AI: `observe` shows `slowed x0.60, rooted, capped 3.0m/s, no sprint, sprint cost x0.00` after the entity's motion; the query tool `move_info`
(`id` optional) gives the modifiers, the walk / run / sprint / swim speeds they leave (a rooted body swims at 0) and the wading depth and factor. Scenario:
`crates/sandbox/scenarios/modifiers.scenario`.

**Input.** The action map turns the keyboard, mouse and gamepad into an `Intent` for the entity with `LocalPlayer`. It is read between ticks (`PreUpdate`); `Intent` is written only when something changes (the replay records every change).

- `InputMap { contexts }`: context (`gameplay`, `menu`, or the game's own) → actions → bindings. A binding is one of: `Key`, `Mouse`,
  `GamepadButton`, `GamepadAxis` (dead zone, scale), `KeyAxis`, `Keys2D` (WASD as a 2D axis), `Buttons2D` (the gamepad's D-pad as a 2D axis), `Stick`,
  `MouseMotion`, `MouseWheel` (this frame's scroll as a 2D axis, `y` away from the player; the standard map binds it to `lock_switch`).
  `Stick` has `deadzone` (radial, the rest rescaled to 0..1), `scale` for both axes, and three optional fields for stick look (C9): `scale_x` / `scale_y` (`Some(3.2)`; a per-axis scale where set, `scale` where absent) and `curve` (the exponent on the magnitude after the dead zone, `m -> m^curve`, direction kept; default 1.0 is linear; it must be above 0 and finite, otherwise a content error names the file; `rebind` and a saved `controls` string are refused the same way). A look stick that turns 3.2 units per second of yaw and 2.0 of pitch (the scale is in the `look` action's units per second) with a 1.6 response is `Stick(stick: Right, deadzone: 0.2, scale_x: Some(3.2), scale_y: Some(2.0), curve: 1.6)`. The new fields are not written while they are default, so every old `input_map` file and saved `controls` string reads and writes as before; `rebind` takes the same text.
  Action mode: `Press` (one press), `Hold` (while held), `Toggle` (a press turns it on until the next press: "hold or press" for accessibility). `directional: true` — a press carries the direction the player is moving in (a roll towards where the stick points). Slot 0 is the main binding; slot 1 and up are spares.
- The context stack `InputContexts`: only the top one fires; `menu` blocks `gameplay` until it is removed.
- Defaults come from content (`*.input_map.ron`, id `default`, hot reload) or from the built-in
  `InputMap::standard`:
  ```ron
  // assets/content/controls.input_map.ron
  { "default": (contexts: [
      (name: "gameplay", actions: [
          (action: "move", bindings: [Keys2D(up: KeyW, down: KeyS, left: KeyA, right: KeyD), Stick(stick: Left)]),
          (action: "jump", bindings: [Key(Space), GamepadButton(South)]),
          (action: "sprint", bindings: [Key(ShiftLeft)], mode: Hold),
          (action: "dodge", bindings: [Key(ControlLeft)], directional: true),
      ]),
  ]) }
  ```
- Rebinding: `rebind` (developer) puts a binding into an action's slot, changes its mode (`mode`) or clears the slot (`unbind`).
  A binding that another action already uses is rejected with that action's name, unless you pass `force`:
  ```text
  $ shards act rebind action=jump binding='Key(KeyE)'
  error: Key(KeyE) is already bound to `interact` in `gameplay`; rebind `interact` first, or force it to take the input over
  $ shards act rebind action=interact binding='Key(KeyG)'
  ok: gameplay/interact: slot 0 = Key(KeyG)
  $ shards act rebind action=jump binding='Key(KeyE)'
  ok: gameplay/jump: slot 0 = Key(KeyE)
  $ shards act rebind action=sprint mode=Toggle
  ok: gameplay/sprint: mode toggle
  ```
  For the player there is a screen: a `Binding` widget in the menu content shows an action's inputs and waits for a new key, mouse button or gamepad button; it does not take an input that is in use, but names the action that holds it (see "UI (E9)", "Keys").
- Saving: the player's changes are settings of the `controls` group (`ControlSettings`), and Bevy's settings save them to `settings.toml`, see "Settings (E8.6)". The file holds only what differs from the defaults (`"gameplay.jump" =
  ["Key(KeyJ)", "GamepadButton(South)"]`, mode in `hold_or_toggle`), so new defaults reach old files too.
  `rebind` and any change to `InputMap` write the difference to the settings (to disk a second later), while `settings_set` and re-read defaults build the map again; the contexts and actions that the game added to the map itself stay
  (the map is rebuilt only from changed keys and modes, not from the defaults as a whole).
  `settings_set` for `controls` checks the same things as `rebind`: the action and context must exist (the error names similar ones and gives the list), no other action of the context may already use the input (`force=true` on `rebind`, the developer tool, takes it by force; for `settings_set` free the input first: the refusal names the call), and putting an entry back to its default must not take an input that another action already uses. It takes the game's own actions and contexts into account, but they cannot be set in the settings; a context with a dot in its name is a content error (`context.action` cannot be split at the dot). `rebind` and
  `input_bindings` right after `settings_set` (with no frame between the calls) see its result. A file entry that cannot be read or does not fit (an action the map does not have, a typo in a key, an unknown mode) does not stop the others: each one is named in the journal, the rest apply, and at the next save the entry stays in the file as it is, so the player does not lose what they wrote. The journal names an input that clashes in the file.
  The old file `input.ron` (`<user settings folder>/<game>/input.ron`) is moved once, and only if the game asked for it: `app.insert_resource(InputSettings::for_game("my_game"))` (`app_name` is the old game's folder, `config_dir` replaces the user folder in tests). So a game without this line does not pick up someone else's shared `~/.config/shards/input.ron`, and the move happens only in a window, where the settings live in the platform folder (not with `--settings-dir`, not in tests and not in a headless run). If the settings do not have controls yet and the file can be read, its content goes into `controls.bindings`, and only after `settings.toml` is written and holds them is the file renamed to `input.ron.imported`; in the journal: `settings: imported the controls from …`. A file that cannot be read or could not be written stays as it is, and the journal gets a warning. An explicit `InputSettings.file` is always read and is never renamed without the settings being written.
- `accessibility.hold_to_toggle` turns hold actions (`sprint`, `block`, `glide`, `crouch`) into toggles: a press holds, the next one releases. The map does not change (its mode stays the same, and `input_bindings` says so).
- `input_bindings` shows which input controls what:
  ```text
  $ shards act input_bindings
  gameplay (active)
    move         Keys2D(up:KeyW,down:KeyS,left:KeyA,right:KeyD) · Keys2D(up:ArrowUp,…) · Stick(stick:Left,deadzone:0.15,scale:1.0)
    jump         Key(Space) · GamepadButton(South)
    sprint       [hold] Key(ShiftLeft) · GamepadButton(LeftThumb)
    …
  other contexts: menu (input_bindings context=NAME)
  ```
- A real gamepad needs the feature `gamepad` (gilrs, needs libudev). Without the feature, `Gamepad` entities work if the game or a test creates them.

**Camera** (`ThirdPersonCamera`, only with a window; the maths without one). Orbit with the mouse and the right stick; collision with walls (a ray from the head to the desired position pulls the camera in); lock-on: the `lock_on` key picks the target closest to the centre of the frame within the cone and range of `CameraSettings::{lock_cone_deg, lock_range}`, a look to one side switches to a neighbour, a target that leaves the range, dies or loses its `LockOnTarget` ends the lock (with a `lock_on` definition the rules of "Lock-on rules (C6)" below decide instead); aim assist, and shake (`AddTrauma`; its strength, and the field of view, sensitivity and Y-axis inversion, come from the player's settings, see "Settings (E8.6)"). The chosen target is written to `Intent.target` between ticks (it is an input, and the replay records it), but the camera never clears someone else's target. **The camera is only a view:** gameplay and `observe` do not read it (`observe` sees through the eyes of the subject), so a window with the camera plays the same game as one without. The first-person camera of F1b, which sits at the eye of the body and writes `Intent.look`, is described in "The first-person camera and the view model (F1b)" after "Look as input (F1a)".

**Camera numbers and offsets (C7).** The camera's feel numbers are not constants in code (the two exceptions are named below: the 30..120 field-of-view limit and the shake's noise frequencies). They are the resource `CameraTuning` (content kind `camera`, `*.camera.ron`, one map of ids to definitions; the camera reads the id `default`, hot-reloaded; without one it runs on the code defaults, which are the numbers it always had, so a game without a camera definition sees no change; a definition that is removed puts the defaults back; a game may also set the resource from code, and content that exists wins whenever it loads or changes). Missing fields take the defaults, unknown ones are an error, and `--check-content` names the file and the field of an out-of-range number. A default serializes to nothing, so adding a field never changes the hash of a definition that does not set it.

| field | default (the old constant) | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `pitch` | `(-0.45, 1.35)` (`PITCH`) | lowest and highest tilt, radians, positive looks down from above; within ±(π/2 − 0.02) |
| `follow_rate` | `None`: each camera's `ThirdPersonCamera::follow_rate` (14) | how fast the focus catches up with the character, 1/s |
| `release_factor` | `1.3` (`RELEASE_FACTOR`) | a lock the camera picked lets go at this many times its range |
| `snap_distance` | `12` (was a constant) | a followed character farther than this from the focus (m) is a jump: the focus lands on it at once |
| `body_snap_distance` | `4` | a body that moved farther than this (m) in one tick was placed, not walked: render interpolation starts over there (see "Render interpolation (C8)") |
| `framing.yaw_rate` / `pitch_rate` | `7` / `7` (`LOCK_FRAMING_RATE`) | how fast a locked camera turns to frame its target, 1/s |
| `framing.pitch_target` | `None`: the pitch of the line from the target to the focus | a fixed pitch to frame at |
| `framing.pitch_clamp` | `(0.15, 0.7)` | the range that geometric pitch is held to |
| `framing.min_horizontal` | `0` (always frames) | nearer than this to the target (m, on the ground, from the focus) the camera stops framing |
| `framing.fit` | `None`: the view looks at the focus | keep the player and a locked target high on a big body in frame together (R4, below); `Some(())` takes the defaults of its fields |
| `framing.fit.margin` / `tilt_max` / `rate` | `0.15` / `0.6` / `6` | how far inside the top and bottom edges the target and the feet are kept (a share of half the frame's height, below 1); the most the view turns up (radians); how fast the turn catches up and goes back after the lock, 1/s |
| `arm.radius` / `arm.min_distance` | `0.25` / `0.7` (`CAMERA_RADIUS`, `MIN_DISTANCE`) | the sphere a wall pulls in; never closer than this to the focus |
| `arm.follow_rate` | `None`: at once | how fast the arm grows back after a wall let go of it, and how fast its nominal length follows `ThirdPersonCamera::distance`, 1/s. It always shortens at once |
| `flick.mouse_threshold_px` | `14` (`FLICK` 0.035 rad at the standard map's 0.0025 rad/px) | horizontal mouse pixels, summed, that switch the lock-on target |
| `flick.mouse_decay_px_s` | `None`: one frame's motion only | how fast the sum drains, px/s |
| `flick.cooldown_s` | `0.35` (`FLICK_COOLDOWN`) | seconds before the next switch |
| `flick.cooldown_on_miss` | `false` | whether a flick that found nobody starts the cooldown |
| `flick.stick_threshold` | `0.75` | right-stick deflection (0..1, after the dead zone) that switches |
| `flick.stick_rearm` | `None`: no latch | the stick must come back below this before it can switch again; a lock taken with the stick already over starts disarmed |
| `trauma.decay` | `1.4` (`TRAUMA_DECAY`, linear) | trauma drained per second |
| `trauma.shift_m` / `pitch_deg` / `yaw_deg` / `roll_deg` | `0.12` / `2` / `2` / `3` | the most a shake of trauma 1 moves and turns the view (scaled by trauma squared) |
| `auto_centre.delay_s` / `rate` / `min_speed` / `max_turn_deg` | `1.5` / `2.5` / `0.5` / `150` | the auto-centre (K2, below; only while the player's `controls.camera_auto_centre` is on): real seconds the look must be left alone; how fast the view turns behind the body, 1/s; the least walking speed on the ground, m/s; a body facing farther than this from the camera's forward (degrees, at most 180) does not swing it round |
| `auto_centre.pitch` | `None`: the pitch stays the player's | a tilt the auto-centre eases toward with the yaw (radians, within `pitch`) |
| `picture.tone_mapping` | `None`: the camera's own (Bevy's `TonyMcMapface`) | how the light the camera draws becomes the picture's colours: `None`, `Linear` (a plain clip), `Reinhard`, `ReinhardLuminance`, `AcesFitted`, `AgX`, `SomewhatBoringDisplayTransform`, `TonyMcMapface`, `BlenderFilmic`, `KhronosPbrNeutral` (the picture, below) |
| `picture.bloom` | `None`: the camera's own (none) | a glow round light brighter than `threshold`; the camera draws in HDR while it is set (the picture, below) |
| `picture.bloom.intensity` / `low_frequency_boost` / `low_frequency_boost_curvature` / `high_pass_frequency` | `0.15` / `0.7` / `0.95` / `1` | Bevy's natural bloom: how strong the glow is, how much more the wide part of it weighs and how that falls off, and how wide it reaches (above 0, at most 1) |
| `picture.bloom.threshold` / `threshold_softness` | `0` / `0` | only light brighter than this spreads (linear; 0 lets everything glow a little, as Bevy's natural bloom does); how soft the knee at the threshold is, 0 to 1 |
| `picture.bloom.composite` | `EnergyConserving` | `EnergyConserving`: the glow takes its share of the light from the picture (Bevy's natural bloom); `Additive`: it is added on top |
| `picture.grading` | `None`: the camera's own | a colour grade of the whole picture: `exposure` (stops), `temperature` and `tint` (white balance, `-1` to `1`), `hue_deg`, `saturation`, `contrast`, `lift`, `gamma` and `gain` (the neutral values: 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1); Bevy's `ColorGrading` with the same values for shadows, midtones and highlights. Bevy grades just before tone mapping, so it shows nothing under `tone_mapping: None`. A grading volume blends the picture away from it and back (the picture, below; "Lights and colour grading (F13)") |
| `mode` | `ThirdPerson` | the camera the game plays through: `FirstPerson` puts a `FirstPersonCamera` on every `ThirdPersonCamera` entity (F1b, "The first-person camera and the view model") |
| `first_person.*` | see the table in "The first-person camera and the view model (F1b)" | the first-person camera's own numbers: the ease on steps, the landing dip, the bob, the lean, the default view model; read by `FirstPersonCamera` only |

The ranges of `pitch`, `follow_rate`, the rates, thresholds and amplitudes are content errors when out of range (a rate must be above 0, a re-arm level below the threshold, and so on). `framing.pitch_clamp` must not have its low end above its high end, and `framing.fit` needs a margin in [0, 1), a `tilt_max` within [0, π/2 − 0.02] and a rate above 0; it may be wider than `pitch`, since the framed pitch is then held to the pitch limits like any other. Two things stay constants on purpose: the engine's 30..120 limit on the field of view (the player's setting is clamped to it too) and the shake's noise frequencies (the look of the noise, not a feel number).

*Smoothing.* Every smoothing is the exact exponential `1 - exp(-rate * dt)` through `bevy::math::ops::exp`, so it does not depend on the frame rate (`damp`, `lock_framing`, `arm_reach`). `critically_damped_step(x, v, target, omega, dt)` is the closed form of a critically damped spring (for a landing dip: kick `v`, aim at 0); one step of `2 dt` equals two of `dt`. *The arm*: a wall pulls it in at once; once it lets go the shortfall below the nominal length shrinks at `arm.follow_rate` (the rate acts on the shortfall, so a plain zoom is smoothed once, by `arm_length`; `ThirdPersonCamera::arm_reach` is where it stood last frame, `arm_length` its nominal length), never past what is free and never closer than `arm.min_distance` (as far as the room allows). A jump of the focus (a teleport) resets it.

*Flick.* The flick thresholds are in raw units, so they are the old constants only at the standard map, mouse sensitivity 1.0 and 60 Hz: before, the mouse flick read the scaled, sensitivity-adjusted axis (0.035 rad) and the stick flick also carried the frame time. Now the player's sensitivity and a binding's scale do not move the flick, and the stick flick does not depend on the frame rate. A stick's flick reads its deflection before its response `curve` and its scales (`scale`, or C9's `scale_x` / `scale_y` per axis), so a look curve or a faster yaw does not move the stick threshold either. An inverted stick binding (a negative scale on that axis) keeps its flipped side. If both devices flick in one frame the mouse wins and the stick is not asked. The mouse is measured in raw pixels and the stick in deflection, both from `ControlState` (`look_pointer_px()`, `look_stick()`); the `look` axis stays the scaled sum. The cooldown runs on the simulation clock, `Time<Virtual>`: a paused game does not run it down, a slowed one runs it down slowly. The mouse's sum drains on the frame clock (`Time<Real>`): that is input, not the game. Follow, framing, arm and shake stay on `Time<Real>`, so a paused game still shows its camera settle. There is no look grace after a spawn. Gameplay reads the stored `ThirdPersonCamera::yaw` (`input` turns the move axes by it): the shake only moves the camera's `Transform`.

*Offsets.* `CameraOffsets` (a resource, neutral by default) is what a game's systems add to the base values; `orbit_camera` reads it after them, every frame: `fov_add_deg` is added to the player's field of view before the engine's 30..120 limit (sprint widening, a finisher's punch); `focus_dip_m` lowers the camera and what it looks at together, so the picture drops without tilting (a landing dip; negative raises); `pitch_min` / `pitch_max` narrow the tuning's pitch range (an override outside it is held to it), and the stored pitch is clamped to the result (a swim cap: the camera stays above the water; lifting the cap does not push the pitch back up); `aiming` says the player aims (what aiming is, a ranged technique or a zoom, is the game's): free look then turns by the player's `aim_sensitivity` instead of `sensitivity` (K1), and a lock frames as it always does. **The writer owns its value**: the system that writes a field sets it on every frame it wants an effect and puts it back to `0.0` / `None` / `false` itself when it is done. The camera only reads: it never decays, sums or stores an offset, and it never writes `CameraSettings`, `ThirdPersonCamera::focus` or the stored pitch except through the clamp above, so an offset stays as its writer left it until the writer puts it back (a writer that stops without resetting
leaves its effect on). Two systems that want the same field must be combined by the game into one writer. Write in `PostUpdate` before `CameraSystems::Orbit` to be seen on the same frame (the set is empty without the `render` feature, so the writers run and are testable headless).

*Auto-centre (K2).* With the player's `controls.camera_auto_centre` on (`CameraSettings::auto_centre`; off by default, so no picture changes until the player asks), free look turns back behind the body it follows once the player leaves the look alone: after `auto_centre.delay_s` real seconds with no look input (`ThirdPersonCamera::look_idle_s`), while the body walks at least `min_speed` on the ground (measured from where the body is drawn, frame to frame: not from the focus, which goes on catching up after the body stops), the yaw eases toward behind the body's facing at `rate` (the exact exponential), and the pitch toward `auto_centre.pitch` when it is set. A body facing more than `max_turn_deg` from the camera's forward (one walking toward the camera) does not swing it round, and one standing still keeps the view. Any look input, a lock, a jump of the focus and a body placed farther than `body_snap_distance` in one frame (a teleport, a respawn; `ThirdPersonCamera::subject_seen`) start the wait over; a lock frames as it always does. The step is `camera::math::auto_centre`; like the rest of the camera it runs on `Time<Real>`, outside the simulation, so nothing in a replay or a snapshot changes. The sandbox has the toggle in its settings' controls.

**Scene cameras (K3).** A shot is a short camera move a game plays over the orbit camera: a scene of half a minute, a boss's entrance of a few seconds (GDD §6.3, §15.1). It is content, kind `shot` (`*.shot.ron`, `shards::motion::camera::ShotDef`; presentation, so it is not in the content hash a replay checks):

```ron
// content/scenes/warden_intro.shot.ron
{
    "warden_intro": (
        keys: [
            (at: 0.0, eye: On(role: "boss", offset: (0.0, 2.0, -7.0), local: true), look: On(role: "boss", offset: (0.0, 3.0, 0.0))),
            (at: 4.0, eye: On(role: "boss", offset: (2.0, 1.0, -4.0), local: true), look: On(role: "boss", offset: (0.0, 4.0, 0.0)),
             fov_deg: 45.0, ease: InOut),
            (at: 4.5, eye: At((0.0, 3.0, 12.0)), look: On(role: "hero"), cut: true),
            (at: 6.0, eye: At((0.0, 2.0, 9.0)), look: On(role: "hero", offset: (0.0, 1.5, 0.0))),
        ],
        blend_in_s: 0.5,   // default 0: the shot starts where its first key is
        blend_out_s: 0.8,  // default 0.5
        skippable: true,   // default
    ),
}
```

- *Keys*: where the camera stands (`eye`) and what it looks at (`look`) at `at` seconds from the start (0 or more, each key strictly later than the one before it, at most 120 s), and optionally the field of view (`fov_deg`, 10 to 120; without one, the player's). Between two keys the camera moves from one to the other, the later key's `ease` (`Linear`, the default, or `InOut`) shaping the move; a `cut` key is jumped to at its time (the camera holds the key before until then). Before the first key the camera holds it; the shot ends at the last.
- *Points*: `At((x, y, z))` is a place in the world; `On(role:, offset:, local:)` a place on a body the game names when it plays the shot: its position where it is drawn (between ticks, as the orbit camera follows it) plus `offset`, turned with the body when `local` (its forward is `-z`). If the body disappears while the shot plays (it is despawned, or loses its `Transform`: a dead enemy taken away), its points stay at the last place it was seen until the shot ends.
- *Playing*: `shards::motion::camera::shot::play(world, id, &roles)` (`roles`: role name → entity) starts it on this machine's camera; `stop` is the game's skip (refused for a shot with `skippable: false`), `cancel` ends any. A shot blends in over `blend_in_s` from what the camera showed and back to where the orbit camera is over `blend_out_s`, at its end or when stopped (from what the camera showed then: a blend in longer than the shot goes back from where it got to); a second `play` ends the first as skipped. `play` is refused, with what to fix, for a shot that is missing or has problems, a role the shot uses with no body given for it, a role given that the shot does not use (both are refused: the roles given must be exactly the shot's), a body that does not exist, and where nothing is drawn: a headless game has no `ThirdPersonCamera`, so a shot only plays in a window or `--offscreen`.
- *The orbit camera meanwhile* stands still: its yaw and pitch stay as they were (the move axes keep their meaning), look input turns nothing, and lock-on picks and switches nothing (a lock the player had is framed again after the shot). Shake and the game's `CameraOffsets` do not touch the shot.
- *Time* is `Time<Virtual>`: the pause menu pauses a shot, a slowed game slows it, and in a game started `--paused` it moves only by `step`. It is drawn in `PostUpdate` after `CameraSystems::Orbit`.
- *Messages*: the observer events `ShotStarted { id }` and `ShotEnded { id, skipped }` (`skipped`: stopped before the last key, or replaced), journal lines `shot ID starts: 6.0s, boss=e5` and `shot ID ends (done|skipped)` (`Local`), and an `observe` line `SHOT warden_intro 2.4/6.0s skippable, roles boss=e5` (or `SHOT warden_intro stopped, back to the orbit camera in 0.3s`). The resource `Shots` says which plays (`Shots::playing`).
- *Tools* (developer): `play_shot id=warden_intro role.boss=e5 role.hero=e1` and `stop_shot` (`force=true` cancels one that is not skippable).
- *What stays the game's*: blocking the player's input during a scene, letterbox bars and subtitles, pausing or slowing the simulation, and which button skips (it calls `stop`).
- `--check-content` names a shot with no keys, a key time below 0, not strictly later than the key before it (two keys at the same time included) or past 120 s, a key whose `eye` and `look` are the same place, a field of view outside 10 to 120, an empty role, a number that is not finite, a blend outside 0 to 10 s, a key without one of its required fields (`at`, `eye`, `look`), and an unknown field on a shot, a key or a point (a misspelt `ofset` for `offset`); the error names the file and the field.

The simulation never reads the camera: nothing of a shot is in a snapshot or a replay.

**The camera next to a big body (R4).** A locked camera looks at the player's head. Next to a body several times the player's height,
a lock point on it (a horn, a core high in its chest; "Lock points (R3)") leaves the top of the frame, while the frame's bottom
third, below the player's feet, stays empty. The measurement (`tests/motion/camera_big.rs`, `measure`, through the real
`orbit_camera`, at the defaults: arm 5.5 m, focus 1.5 m, 70°): the feet sit at y −0.37 of the frame (−1 bottom, 1 top), and a
point 6 m up at 2 m ahead, 9 m up at 8 m and 12 m up at any distance reach its top edge or pass it. A `framing.fit` keeps both: the camera stands
where the framing puts it, but its view turns up from the focus about its own horizontal axis (`ThirdPersonCamera::tilt`,
`fit_tilt`) just far enough to put the target on the top margin, and never so far that the feet leave the bottom margin; when
both cannot be kept, the player is. Both are measured in the camera's own frame, so a target off to the side (a camera still
turning to a new lock) lands where the frame's height says. The turn eases toward the target at `fit.rate`, but the feet's limit
and `tilt_max` (`fit_room`) hold it on every frame: a wall that shortens the arm or a lower `tilt_max` never lets the feet out (the player and the threat, not the whole silhouette). With the defaults a point fits up
to about 9 m at 2 m ahead, 10 m at 4 m, and 12 m from 6 m out. The fit never tilts the view below the focus, a target the frame
already holds (a body of a person's height, framed at its chest) gives the very same camera as without a fit, and after the lock
the view comes back to the focus at `fit.rate`. A lower camera needs no new number: `framing.pitch_clamp`'s low end is how far
down the framed arm may go (`(0.0, 0.7)` keeps it level with the head next to a big body). Without a `fit` nothing changes. The
lock pick and the flick read the camera's `Transform`, so with a tilt they measure from what the player sees. The far plane
(Bevy's default 1000 m) did not need a number. The sandbox's `combat/camera.camera.ron` turns the fit on for its colossus.

**The picture (`picture`).** The camera content can also say how the picture is drawn: its tone mapping, its bloom and its colour grade (`shards::motion::camera::{PictureTuning, ToneMapping, BloomTuning, BloomComposite, Grading}`). All three are left out by default, and then every camera keeps what the game spawned it with, so a game without a `picture` sees no change. They apply to every 3D camera with `ThirdPersonCamera` or `FirstPersonCamera`, a camera spawned later included. A bloom makes the camera draw in HDR (Bevy's `Bloom` requires `Hdr`): the materials' colours are no longer stopped at full, and tone mapping moves from each material's shader to one pass over the whole picture, so light brighter than white (a lamp, an effect with an `intensity` above 1, see "Effects and decals") keeps its brightness until the tone mapping and the bloom see it. Taking `bloom` out of the content (or the whole definition) gives the camera back its own bloom, or none, and leaves HDR off again if the content turned it on. The same holds for `tone_mapping`. A game that sets its own `Bloom`, `Hdr` or `Tonemapping` on the camera keeps them while the content says nothing. The picture changes nothing else: the `camera` kind is not simulation content, so no replay changes. With HDR on, everything is tone mapped once, in the post pass, particles included (the particles' shader has no tone mapping of its own, so without HDR their colours reach the screen as written).

```ron
// assets/content/combat/camera.camera.ron: the sandbox's bloom; only light 1.5 times past white glows, so nothing
// lit by the sun does, only effects with an `intensity`
{ "default": (picture: (bloom: Some((intensity: 0.3, threshold: 1.5, composite: Additive)))) }
```

**Lock-on rules (C6).** With a `lock_on` definition (content kind `lock_on`, `*.lock_on.ron`, the id `default` (another id is a content error: the engine reads no other), hot reload; `shards::motion::camera::LockOnDef`), lock-on is a simulation rule rather than the camera's: the camera, the `lock_on` tool and the check of every lock use the same plain functions (`shards::motion::camera::lock`), so a window and a headless run decide alike. Without one, everything above holds as it was (the camera's own pick, switch and release, no check), and a game sees no change; the sandbox has one, the template none.

```ron
// assets/content/combat/lock.lock_on.ron (every field is optional: these are the defaults)
{ "default": (range: 30.0, weights: (distance: 1.0, screen: 1.0, view: 0.5, danger: 0.5, current: 0.3),
              aim_height: 0.6, eye_height: 0.9, obstruction_s: Some(2.0), switch_dead_band: 0.05, switch_min_distance: 0.1, frustum: true) }
```

| field | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `range` | `30` | m, in 3D between the two bodies' positions: the pick and the switch look this far, and a lock farther than this is lost |
| `weights.distance` | `1` | the pick's score (lower wins): distance per `range` |
| `weights.screen` | `1` | the angle from the centre of the view to the aim point, per half the view's width (a body's own eyes: per half turn) |
| `weights.view` | `0.5` | the angle on the ground between where the one locking looks and the candidate, from the one locking, per half turn |
| `weights.danger` | `0.5` | taken off for a candidate whose attack would land on the one locking now (its hit zone, `zones_threatening`) |
| `weights.current` | `0.3` | taken off for the current target, so a pick made while locked keeps it unless another is clearly better |
| `aim_height` / `eye_height` | `0.6` / `0.9` | the target's aim point and the locker's eye, as fractions of the body's collider from its bottom (1.8 m without one); a lock point (a body part, R3) is aimed at its centre |
| `obstruction_s` | `Some(2.0)` | a target hidden behind the world (a `WORLD` ray from the eye to the aim point, both bodies left out) this long in a row is lost; counted in ticks (120 at 60 Hz); `None`: never |
| `switch_dead_band` | `0.05` | rad: a switch takes only a candidate past this angle on the side asked for |
| `switch_min_distance` | `0.1` | m on the ground: nearer than this to the locker, a candidate has no direction and is never switched to |
| `frustum` | `true` | the camera picks inside its frustum at the player's base field of view (`CameraSettings::fov_deg`, never the sprint's `CameraOffsets::fov_add_deg`) and the projection's aspect; `false`: the cone `CameraSettings::lock_cone_deg` |
| `wheel_threshold` | `0` | the wheel axis' units (a line for a wheel, the pixels a touchpad sends): a scroll of this much or less in a frame counts as the wheel standing still, so a touchpad's tremor is no turn; `0` takes every turn (the behaviour before it was a number) |

- *Pick* (`pick_lock`, `lock_score`): among the bodies the locker may lock on to (`LockHooks::lockable`; the action module: alive, and `LockOnTarget` or a fighter of another team) within `range` that it can see, the lowest score, the lower `AiId` on a tie. The camera looks from its own eye along its view (inside the frustum or the cone, a clear ray from the camera); the `lock_on` tool without `target` from the body's eye along its facing.
- *Switch* (`switch_lock`, `switch_target`): measured from the locker, not the camera: the signed angle around up from the direction to the current target to each candidate's (left positive); `right` takes those past `-switch_dead_band`, `left` past `+switch_dead_band`; the nearest angle wins, then the lower `AiId`; only what the locker's eye sees. It is the press `lock_switch` (`input_names::LOCK_SWITCH`, `dir.x` the side: `+1` right), used up by `LockSystems::Switch` (`SimSet::Act`, before `MotionSystems::Intent`, so the body faces the new target on that tick; it works without a definition too, by the defaults with `CombatTuning::lock_on_range`). The camera sends it for a look flick (C7's flick thresholds and cooldown; only when the rule finds somebody on that side) and for the mouse wheel (toward the player is right; one switch per turn of the wheel: after a switch the wheel must stand still for a frame, so a touchpad's long or coasting scroll is one switch; the cooldown holds it too); the tool is `lock_on side=left|right`. `lock_switch` is read as an axis: bind it to `MouseWheel()`, `KeyAxis(neg: KeyQ, pos: KeyE)`, a `GamepadAxis` or a `Stick`. A button bound to it is refused with an error that names these: by `InputMap::rebind` (the `rebind` tool), by the controls settings (`settings_set`, a saved file) and by the content check of an `input_map` (`Binding::refused_for`); a keyboard "next target" action is a later addition if a game asks. The standard map binds the wheel to it in every game; without a definition the camera does not read it, so the wheel does nothing there.
- *Check* (`LockSystems::Check`, `SimSet::Cleanup` after `CoreSystems::ClearPresses`, so after the tick's deaths and the engine's despawns, such as the co-op body whose rejoin grace is over, in `AiId` order): every body's `Intent.target` is checked, the player's and every agent-driven body's alike (an NPC brain keeps its own target and does not write `Intent.target`), so an agent that steers a monster through `lock_on` loses that lock to a wall too. A lock is lost when its target is gone, dead (`Dead`), beyond `range` or hidden for `obstruction_s`, and let go of (`e5 lock released: e6`) when its target stops being something the locker may lock on to by the pick's own rule (`LockHooks::lockable`: an ally, a body that is neither a fighter of another team nor a `LockOnTarget`), so an ally a co-op client sends as its target, or a game system sets, does not stay: the host checks it like any other body's. A `lock_on` definition with errors is not in force (the game runs as without one until the content is fixed). A game system that despawns a body that may be locked on to runs before the check (`.before(LockSystems::Check)`, or before `ClearPresses`), so the lock goes on that tick; one after it leaves a lock on nobody, and `action.lock_on_valid` stops the game; `LockSight { target, ticks, secs }` is on the locker only while its target is hidden (it is in the replay and the snapshot), and a tick in sight takes it away, so the count starts again. The camera lets go of a lock only when the player cancels it.
- *Journal*: `e5 lock lost: e6 dead` (`gone`, `out of range (31.0m > 30.0m)`, `obstructed 2.0s`); `e5 locks e6` from the `lock_on` tool and `e5 lock released: e6` from its `off` (from the camera, the same texts as `local` lines: a replay sets the target from the recorded input, without the camera); `e5 locks e7 (switched right from e6)`. *`observe` and `inspect`*: `lock e6`, and `lock e6 (obstructed 0.8s)` while hidden.
- *The tool*: with a definition, `lock_on target=eN` is refused for what the check would take away at once (a dead target, one beyond `range`) and for what the pick would never name (yourself, an ally or anything else that is neither a fighter of another team nor a `LockOnTarget`, a body with no position). Without one an id is taken as before. `lock_on point=NAME` takes a lock point of a big body (see "Lock points (R3)").
- *The rule* `action.lock_on_valid`: with a definition, no body's `Intent.target` names a missing or dead entity after a tick (a game system after `LockSystems::Check` that sets one, or that despawns a body that is locked on to, breaks it).
- *Co-op*: `Intent.target` and the `lock_switch` press are input; the check and the switch run where the simulation runs, never in a client's prediction. A client takes over a lock its host changed (lost, switched, taken by an attack order) once the host has every held state it sent (`InputCapture::adopt_target`): otherwise its next state would put the old target back. Stand scenario `crates/sandbox/scenarios/stand/lock_on.scenario`; single-game scenario `crates/sandbox/scenarios/lock_on.scenario`.
**Render interpolation (C8).** The simulation steps at 60 Hz and a body's `Transform` is the value of the last tick, so on a 144 Hz display a body would move in 60 Hz steps and the follow camera would inherit them. `shards_motion::interp` draws bodies between their last two ticks. It is presentation only: it never writes a body's `Transform` (physics reads it), and it adds nothing to a simulated entity.

- **Where the state lives.** `Interpolated` sits on a *visual child* of a `CharacterController` body (the model, a held prop: any child without an `AiId`); the engine adds it by itself (`adopt_visuals`, `PostUpdate`), so a game that dresses its bodies with a model child needs no code. `NotInterpolated` on a child opts it out. Adoption is opt-out on purpose (a game gets smooth models without code; the few children gameplay reads carry `AiId` or `NotInterpolated`). `body_snap_distance` stays in the `camera` kind for now: it is presentation tuning, and that kind is non-simulation (`SIMULATION = false`), so it never enters a replay's content check. It has no `AiId` and is not in snapshots, replays or the state audit.
- **Capture** (`FixedLast`, `InterpSystems::Capture`): the parent's pose after the tick becomes `current`, the old one `previous`. **Blend** (`PostUpdate`, before transform propagation, `InterpSystems::Blend`): the child's local `Transform` is its own rest transform moved by `lerp/slerp(previous, current, Time<Fixed>::overstep_fraction()) - current` in the body's frame (`visual_offset`). The rest transform is whatever the game left on the child; a change made by someone else is taken as the new rest. The animation clip's own look-ahead (`Time<Fixed>` overstep in the bridge) is separate, so the body trails the tick by up to one step as usual for interpolation.
- **The follow camera** runs after the blend (`CameraSystems::Orbit` is `.after(InterpSystems::Blend)`) and follows the same blended pose (`shown_translation`), for the followed body and for a locked target; with nothing blended it uses the tick value as before.
- **Resets, so a jump is never smeared.** The history starts over when: the body moved farther than `CameraTuning::body_snap_distance` (content, `camera` kind, default 4 m) between two ticks (a respawn, a region change that moves the player to a gate); `MotionState::placed` shows the controller found the feet somewhere it did not leave them (noted in `FixedFirst`, before the controller consumes it); the body's `Transform` is not what the last tick left when a frame is drawn (a `teleport` between frames: shown at once); the tick counter did not advance by one between captures (a snapshot loaded, a replay rewound, the setting was off). A snapshot load or a region change that replaces an entity gives its new child no history. The engine has no teleport event, so these signals are what it has.
- **Where it does nothing.** Without a picture (headless, simulation tests: `EngineConfig::draws()` is false); with `graphics.interpolation = false` (children go back to exactly the transform the game gave them, so the picture is the old one); while the clock is paused (and after a `step`, which runs ticks without frames): the last tick is drawn, so `shot` agrees with `observe`.
- **Co-op.** A client's remote bodies already blend host states (`shards_net` interp, which shows them a little in the past). Render interpolation applies on a client only to the body it predicts (`Predicted`); the others are left to the net, because blending twice would lag them. The host and single player blend all their bodies.
- **Setting.** `graphics.interpolation` (default `true`) in `GraphicsSettings`; `settings_set group=graphics key=interpolation value=false` is the A/B in a running game.
- **Rules for children and writers.** Every unmarked non-`AiId` child of a body is adopted, so a child that gameplay reads (a weapon socket, a muzzle, an aim origin) must carry an `AiId` or `NotInterpolated`. `restore_rest` (`FixedFirst`) puts blended children back at rest for each tick, so a local `Transform` read in the simulation is exact, on or off; a `GlobalTransform` read in `FixedUpdate` still holds the last picture. A system that rewrites a child's `Transform` must write all of it, before `InterpSystems::Blend` (a partial write is taken as the new rest and drifts); the body must be top-level (a body with a parent is not blended). A child is looked at when its body's `Children` change; one that loses `NotInterpolated` later is not adopted until then. Capture is not ordered against other `FixedLast` systems: one that moves a body after it makes the history start over each tick (no smoothing, never a wrong picture). `body_snap_distance` lives in the `camera` kind but is read by interpolation even without a camera. Pausing the virtual clock (menus, `step`) shows the last tick, so the picture steps by up to one tick of lag at pause and at resume. On a client, `shards_net`'s correction smoothing of the predicted body is applied to its `Transform` and so is not a second layer.

**Warnings about attacks off screen** (E2.6): `threat_indicators(world, viewer, forward)` from the combat module gives, for each attack zone, a direction for the indicator; markers at the edge of the screen are drawn by `shards_action::render::hud` (see "Actions and combat (E3)").

**Movement tools** (player, only through `Intent`):

| tool | what it does |
|---|---|
| `move_to` | walk to an entity or to a point `{x, z}`; `within`, `queue`; `path=true` follows the route from `path_to` |
| `move`, `stop` | walk N metres by compass (N = −Z, E = +X); stop. `move`, `move_to`, `stop`, `jump`, `sprint` and `glide` refuse a dead body with the text every action tool gives (``you are dead; a dev agent can `heal` you``), and a death drops the orders the body held (`Intent.orders`, and the `move_dir` they set; a body with no orders keeps its `Intent`, which its keyboard or brain rewrites every tick), so nothing runs after a `heal`; a downed body (B5) is refused them with its own words (`you are down: ...`) and drops its orders when it goes down, so nothing runs after a revive |
| `jump`, `sprint`, `glide` | jump (out of water, onto the shore); sprint and glide as a state that is on (`on=false` turns it off) |
| `crouch` | hold the crouch, or let go with `hold=false` (F2, "Crouching (F2)"): the capsule comes down (up from the feet in the air), the answer says how far and over how long, and a stand-up under a ceiling says that it waits; a body whose `locomotion` has no `crouch_height` is refused with that reason. A dead or downed body is refused it as it is the rest of the movement tools |
| `look` | where you look (F1a, "Look as input"): `yaw=` and/or `pitch=` in degrees, `at=eN [part=NAME]`, `clear=true`; `observe` then has an `AIM` line |
| `lock_controls`, `unlock_controls` (developer) | the control lock (F12, "Control lock"): `lock_controls [id=] [reason=] [movement=true] [actions=true] [at= deg=]`, `unlock_controls [id=] [reason=NAME or all=true]` |
| `clearance` | query: how far in the eight directions, and what will stop you; `stance=` (F2: `standing`, `crouched` or `current`, the default) measures with that size of body |
| `move_info` | query: what modifies a character's movement (slow, caps, root, stance, rates, sprint cost), the walk, run, sprint and swim speeds they leave, and the wading depth |
| `path_to` | query: the route over what can be walked, swum and climbed; `stance=` as `clearance` (a crouched route is planned on the local grid: the navmesh is baked for the standing body) |
| `input_bindings` (player), `rebind` (developer) | controls; `rebind` writes to the `controls` settings |
| `physics_overlay` (developer, window) | colliders and volumes |
| `camera_mode` (developer, a query) | `mode=first`, `third` or `content` (F1b): look through the first-person camera or the orbit one for this session, or leave it to the `camera` content; without `mode`, says which |

**An order that makes no progress ends** (`shards_motion::orders`). A `move` or `move_to` order whose body has not come closer to its goal (flat distance) by 0.1 m (`STALL_PROGRESS`) for 2 s (`STALL_SECONDS`) is dropped as `blocked`: the steering is zeroed, the event `OrderEnded` is triggered, the journal says `e1 move_to (20.0, 0.0) ended: blocked (no closer than 0.10 m in 2.0 s)`, and `observe` shows `last order ended: move_to (20.0, 0.0): blocked` on the body until its next order starts (the lazy component `OrderProgress`; snapshots keep it, replay checks leave it out since the queue itself is checked). The orders behind it run on. A sprint order against a wall no longer drains the stamina for ever. The count waits while the body is not free to walk (an action holds it: `LocomotionInput.locked`, or a push moves it: `external`, or a control lock takes its movement away: F12, the order waits for the lock to lift), and restarts at every 0.1 m gained, so a slow walk (a crawl of 0.05 m/s is enough), a guard, a stagger, a walk round a corner and a route (`path=true` is one order per leg, each with its own count) are never ended. An order to an *entity* also counts a body that moves at least 0.1 m while its target moves at least 0.1 m too (a chase of a target that runs away is not blocked; a body that circles a target that stands still, or one that is wedged while its target runs, is). When several bodies stall on the same tick the journal lines come in `AiId` order. It runs in the simulation only; a client's orders are ended by its host. The movement tools also refuse a dead body (``you are dead; a dev agent can `heal` you``), and a death drops the orders.
