Quads are unshaded anyway; with `glow` it changes nothing. `intensity: 1.0` — how bright the colour is: its light (linear, after sRGB) times this, so `2.0` is twice the light of `color`. Above 1 a colour goes past white, which only a camera that draws in HDR keeps (the camera's `picture.bloom`, see "Camera numbers and offsets"): there it stays bright through the tone mapping and the bloom spreads a glow round it. Without HDR each channel stops at full, so white gets no brighter and a colour brightens only in the channels that were below full. `0` is black.
- `shape` — `Quad` (a soft spot, turned towards the camera; the default), `Cube` or `Shard` (a shard): these are lit from above and tumble at a rate of `spin: 360.0` (degrees per second, each particle has its own share of it). `Disc` — a flat round disc `size` across that lies level and never turns (a shockwave, a ripple): give it `speed: (0.0, 0.0)` and let `size_end` open it.
- `offset: (0.0, 1.0, 0.0)` — where they start, as an offset from the entity's feet or from the point; `radius: 0.5` — the particles are born in a sphere of this radius.
- `push: (1.0, 1.0)` — the share of a play's push (`PlayOptions::push`, `PlayEffect::push`, `effect_play push=[…]`: a velocity in m/s, such as a body's run or the way of a roll) that each particle adds to its velocity; `(0.6, 1.0)` scatters it. A play without a push draws no number for it.
- `strength` — how a play's strength (`play_scaled`, a cue's `strength`, `PlayEffect::strength`, `effect_play strength=…`) changes the particles: `(count_per: 6.0, speed: true, size: true)`. `count_per` — particles more for each 1 of strength above 1 (fewer below): a burst starts `count + count_per × (strength − 1)`, rounded down (`count: 12, count_per: 6.0` is `int(6 + 6 × strength)`; `0.0` always `count`); left out, `count × strength`, rounded and at least one. `speed: true` — each particle's starting speed times the strength. `size: true` (the default) — its size times the strength. Left out entirely, it is what a scaled play always did: the number and the size, not the speed. What a `rate` emits later follows the strength in proportion.
- `mesh: "models/chunk.glb"` (F9) — a glTF mesh drawn for each particle in place of its `shape`; `image: "textures/leaf.png"` — a picture a `Quad` wears (its colour times the picture's, its shape the picture's alpha). `collide: true` — the particles land: each is stepped against the world's `WORLD` colliders, bounces (`restitution: 0.4`, 0 to 1), slides (`friction: 0.6`) and comes to rest; `rest: UntilCleared` keeps it there past the 30 s cap until it is cleared (the default `Fade` is the particle's own life); `tags: ["gore"]` — what `shards_fx::clear` takes the effect's particles away by. All of it is in "Gore: marks and debris (F9)" below; an effect that names none of them is as it was.
- `max_live: 64` — the size of the pool (up to 4096): the effect creates this many meshes once, and it never has more live particles than that.

**The `fx` table.** `effects` maps an engine event to an effect; `cues` maps a clip label (`AnimationCue`: `footstep`, `swoosh`) to an effect, on the body (its feet), or at the world position of the cue's `bone` when the clip's cue names one (`EffectAt::Point`; the effect's `offset` still adds to it), with the cue's `strength` scaling the burst and the particles' size (and what a `rate` emits later, over the same `duration`): `shards::fx::play_scaled(world, …, strength)`, which `play` calls at 1; at 0 nothing plays;
a label with no entry plays the effect of its own name, if there is one. Events: `damaged` (on the one who was hit), `blocked`, `parried`, `evaded`,
`guard_broken` (on the defender), `staggered`, `died`, `healed` (on the one it happened to), `telegraph` (on the attacker), and for F9 `shot_impact` (a shot stopped at a world surface: at the point, `aim: Surface` sends the particles out along its normal), `shot_hit` (a shot went through a body: at the point, back towards the shooter) and `part_broken` (a body part broke off: at the part, back towards the attacker; `aim: Away` sends chunks on). A fourth map of the table, `marks`, lays spots on surfaces from events (see "Gore: marks and debris (F9)" below). An event with an
attacker plays the effect on the side of the body that faces the attacker (at the edge of the collider), and `aim: Hit` sends the particles from there back toward the
attacker; such an effect plays at the point and does not follow the body. The game plays its own effect with the event
`commands.trigger(PlayEffect::new("coin_sparkle", EffectAt::Entity(chest)))` (`shards::fx::{PlayEffect, EffectAt}`) (or `EffectAt::Point`, `.toward(dir)` — the axis for
`aim: Hit`, `.strength(1.5)`, `.push(velocity)`), or with the function `shards::fx::play(world, …)`, which returns how many particles started (`play_with(world, effect, at, PlayOptions { toward, strength, push })` for all of them at once).

**Particles.** The engine has its own particles, which run on the CPU (`bevy_hanabi` has no version for Bevy 0.20). Each effect has a pool of `max_live` meshes. They are made when the content loads (and again when the effect is changed), and they are hidden while free. A play takes the free ones; when none are free, it takes the oldest. All particles of an effect share one mesh and one material. Each particle's colour is in its `MeshTag`, so Bevy draws them in batches. A particle's position is a function of its age (the flight under gravity and drag is solved with a formula, not with steps), on the **simulation clock** (`Time<Fixed>` and its remainder). A pause freezes the sparks; `step` moves them by as many ticks as have passed; in real time they fly along with the ticks. A snapshot that sets the time back removes the particles that were born "later". The pools and particles are entities without an `AiId`: replay, snapshot and co-op do not see them. A co-op client plays the effects of the events that the host sends it, on its own.

**Telegraph decals.** An attack warning on the ground is a decal under it (Bevy's `ForwardDecal` with the module's zone material, a shader in WESL).
The zone's shape in the decal's square is a circle, a cone sector, a box's rectangle, a line, or a capsule's "stadium". The zone is pale, with stripes at 45° to the world axes, and it gets lighter toward the edge. The stripes get denser as the hit comes (`hatch_far` → `hatch_near`, like the gizmo's hatching) and converge on the point the fill grows from. They are counted from that point, not from the origin of the world, so no more stripes pass that point than fit across the zone, however far from the world origin the zone lies. The copy of the zone grows from its middle (the centre of the footprint, like the gizmo ring) as the hit gets closer (`TelegraphStyle::horizon`, as for the gizmo), with a bright edge. At the moment of the hit it covers the zone and flickers (the flicker follows the accessibility setting `flashes`). The colour is as for the gizmo: warm for an enemy's attack, cold for an ally's. The decal lies on whatever is under it, and fades out by 0.6 m in height from its plane (the ground, and the legs of those standing in the zone, not walls and bodies). While decals are on, the gizmos draw only the outline, the symbol and its stem; the hatching and the growing ring go to the decals (`TelegraphStyle::decals`). Decals need the scene's depth: each camera with `AiCamera` gets a `DepthPrepass` while they are on (and loses it when they are switched off, if the module gave it; the camera's own prepass stays). That is one extra depth pass per frame. `telegraph_decals on=false` brings back the gizmos' fill. Decals also come from a pool: one entity per zone, and the spare ones are hidden.

**For agents.** `effects` (Dev, query) lists the effects (what and how many, colours, life, axis, gravity, pool: live/size), the table of events and cues, and the decals on the ground now: whose attack, shape, size, and how far the fill has grown. `effect_play effect=hit_spark at=e6` (or
`point=[4, 0, -2]`, `toward=[1, 0, 0]` for `aim: Hit`, `strength=1.5`, `push=[0, 0, 3]`; Dev, control) plays the effect and replies how many particles started and how many are alive in the
pool. `telegraph_decals on=false` (Dev, query; without an argument it turns them on) switches the decals. The setting is the resource `FxSettings`, not part of the
replay or the snapshot. `mark_spawn` and `fx_clear` (marks and landing particles), and the marks and debris lines of `effects`, are in "Gore: marks and debris (F9)" below.

Without rendering, `effects` says `11 effects · nothing is drawn headless: effects play in a window or with --offscreen · telegraph
decals on` and lists the effects with their pool sizes, and `effect_play` refuses: ``nothing is drawn headless: effects play in a window
or with --offscreen (effect `hit_spark` is known)``; events then play nothing. For an effect that is not in the content, `effect_play`
suggests the nearest name (``no effect `hit_sprak` (did you mean `hit_spark`?)``), and `PlayEffect` writes to the journal once
(`fx: PlayEffect: no effect …`). `ai/status` has the field `fx`: `{"effects": 11, "live": 36, "decals": 2, "telegraph_decals": true, "marks": 0, "debris": {"resting": 0, "flying": 0}, "rays": {"last": 0, "max": 0, "total": 0, "budget": 2048}}` (the last three are the gore's performance counters). In the developer menu there is the item `effects` ("Effects, their pools and decals", section `world`) and the switch `telegraph_decals` ("Telegraphs as
decals on the ground", section `combat`).

**Checking the content.** `--check-content` and `content_check` name the file, the effect and the field:

```text
content/fx/sandbox.effect.ron: effect `smoke`: one play starts 40 particles and max_live keeps 8: raise max_live to 40 at least, or a play takes back its own first particles
content/fx/sandbox.effect.ron: effect `smoke`: lifetime: (min, max) with min above 0 and at most max, not (0.8, 0.2)
content/fx/sandbox.effect.ron: effect `smoke`: color: `grey` is not a colour: `#rrggbb` or `#rrggbbaa`
content/fx/sandbox.fx.ron: fx `sandbox`: effects: no engine event `damged` (did you mean `damaged`?); events: damaged, blocked, …
content/fx/sandbox.fx.ron: fx `sandbox`: effects.damaged -> unknown effect `hit_sprak` (did you mean `hit_spark`?)
```

Also checked: an effect that starts no particles (neither `count` nor `rate` with `duration`), `spread` outside 0…360, `lift` outside −90…90, negative `drag`, `size_end`, `radius`, `swell`, a `size_ease` that is not above 0, a `push` range out of order, a `count_per` that is no number, a negative `intensity`, `max_live` outside 1…4096, a second `fx` table in the game, an empty cue label. An effect with an error on its first load still plays (like any definition that was read), but within the limits that the check names: the pool is at most 4096 meshes, one play starts at most 1024 particles, a `rate` of at most 4096, and a particle lives at most 30 s. A typo such as `max_live: 4000000000` or `rate: 5e9` does not hang the game; the check names it (`one play starts 4294967295 particles …`).

**How the game uses it.** (1) The effects are in `assets/content/*.effect.ron`, and the table is one `*.fx.ron`. The sandbox has the hit and block sparks (shard particles), the parry flash, the death dust (cubes), the heal glow, a broken guard's ring (a `Disc`) and a kick's dust (`swell`, `push`, a `strength` response) that the game plays with a push. The template has the hit and block sparks and the death dust. (2) Its own moments are `PlayEffect` from the game's code, or the clip labels in `cues`. (3) To see it: `cargo sandbox --offscreen --paused --port 0
--port-file F &`, `shards act god`, `shards step 1800 --until "journal:winds up"`, `shards shot -o shots/fx.png` — in the picture, the decal under the attack and the sparks on the hit.

**What is missing.** Particles run on the CPU, so tens of thousands alive at once are too much for them (an effect's pool is up to 4096). Particles have no animated sprites, no trails, no light from the particles, and no sound (sound is the audio module); a picture (`image`), a mesh (`mesh`) and a landing on the world (`collide`) are F9's. A telegraph's decal projects straight down, within 0.6 m: on a steep slope its edge fades; the spots of F9 (blood, holes, tracks) are marks, which lie on any surface, see below. Checked on the GPU with `--offscreen` (the `offscreen` test in pixels and the sandbox's screenshots); it has not been checked by eye in a window on a display.

### Gore: marks and debris (F9)

Blood on a wall, a hole where a shot stopped, the chunks of a part that broke off that bounce and stay where they land: `shards_fx` lays spots on surfaces (the `mark` kind) and lets particles come to rest (`collide`). It is all the picture's: it needs the `render` feature and a window or `--offscreen`, its entities have no `AiId`, nothing of it is in a replay or a snapshot, and a machine that draws nothing lays nothing (the tools say so). How a spot looks, how much of it there can be and which event lays it are content; the engine has no blood in it. A death is a death clip, chunks and marks: there are no ragdolls and no rigid bodies.

![A first-person room in the sandbox: a wall behind a dummy that was shot, a bullet hole and blood on the wall, a pool of blood on the floor](media/gore-room.png)

*The sandbox's gore room (`content/fx/gore.*.ron`) seen with `shards shot` from `--offscreen`: shots at a dummy from the side, the splatters on the wall behind it, a pool under it, holes where shots stopped, and the chunks of its head on the floor.*

```ron
// crates/sandbox/assets/content/fx/gore.mark.ron (abbreviated)
{
    "bullet_hole": (texture: "textures/marks/bullet_hole.png", size: (0.1, 0.16), lifetime: Secs(120.0), fade_out: 30.0,
        max_live: 96, roughness: 0.95, tags: ["gore"]),
    "blood_splat": (texture: "textures/marks/blood_splat.png", color: "#7a1014", size: (0.25, 0.6), fade_in: 0.25, max_live: 64,
        roughness: 0.3, tags: ["gore", "blood"]),
    "blood_pool": (color: "#5c0b0e", size: (0.4, 0.8), fade_in: 1.5, max_live: 32, tags: ["gore", "blood"]),
}
// crates/sandbox/assets/content/fx/gore.effect.ron (abbreviated)
{
    "meat_chunk": (count: 5, mesh: "models/chunk.glb", collide: true, restitution: 0.35, friction: 0.7, rest: UntilCleared,
        aim: Away, lift: 35.0, spread: 90.0, speed: (2.0, 5.5), gravity: -9.8, lifetime: (3.0, 3.0), size: (0.08, 0.16),
        size_end: 1.0, color: "#7a2a2a", color_end: "#7a2a2a", max_live: 48, tags: ["gore"]),
}
// crates/sandbox/assets/content/fx/sandbox.fx.ron (the links)
{
    "sandbox": (
        effects: {"shot_impact": "wall_chips", "shot_hit": "blood_spray", "part_broken": "meat_chunk", /* the rest as before */},
        marks: {
            "shot_impact": [(mark: "bullet_hole")],
            "shot_hit": [(mark: "blood_splat", place: Behind(8.0), count: 2, spread: 14.0)],
            "damaged": [(mark: "blood_pool", place: Below(2.5), offset: (0.0, 1.0, 0.0))],
            "part_broken": [(mark: "blood_splat", place: Behind(8.0), offset: (0.0, 0.2, 0.0))],
        },
    ),
}
```

**Marks (the `mark` kind, `*.mark.ron`, not simulation content).** A definition is one kind of spot; its id is what a link, `spawn_mark` and `mark_spawn` name. All fields are optional; a field that does not exist is an error that names the line.

- `texture: "textures/marks/bullet_hole.png"` — a PNG inside the assets folder. The mark's colour times the picture's, its shape is the picture's alpha: make the picture white (or any grey) on clear, with a clear border, and the colour makes it blood. Without one the mark is a soft round spot.
- `color: "#7a1014"` (`#rrggbb` or `#rrggbbaa`, sRGB; the alpha is how opaque it is at most) and `size: (0.25, 0.6)` — its width in metres, a range: each mark draws its own.
- `rotate: true` — each mark is turned at random about the surface's normal; off, its picture stands upright on a wall (any way up on a floor or a ceiling).
- `fade_in: 0.25` — seconds a mark takes to show in full (a pool that spreads in); `fade_out: 30.0` — seconds before its end that a `Secs` mark fades out.
- `lifetime: Secs(120.0)` or `UntilCleared` (the default) — on the simulation's clock (a pause freezes it). `UntilCleared` keeps a mark until the cap recycles it for a newer one, `shards_fx::clear` or a new world takes it.
- `max_live: 64` — the cap of the kind (1 to 4096): a pool per kind; one mark more takes the place of the **oldest laid** (marks laid in one tick are told apart by their order).
- `depth: 0.15` — how far off the decal's plane (m) a surface still takes the paint, fading. A small number keeps a mark on the surface it was laid on and off a body that stands in front of it; a large one lets it wrap round a corner or a step.
- `roughness: 0.9` (0 wet and shining, 1 dry), `unlit: true` (its own colour in any light) — the standard material's.
- `tags: ["gore"]` — what `clear` takes the kind away by.

**How a mark is drawn.** The telegraph decals are Bevy's `ForwardDecal` (a quad that the shader projects onto what the depth prepass shows within a distance of the quad's plane), with a material of the module's own (an unlit zone). The projector is not tied to the ground: its quad takes any rotation, and the shader projects along the quad's own normal. A mark reuses it with its quad turned so that its +Y is the surface's normal (`Mark::rotation`), a hair (2 mm) off the surface, and so lies on a wall, a ceiling or a floor alike; the telegraph's "straight down, within 0.6 m" belongs to its own material and its quad lying level, not to the projector. What a mark does not reuse is the zone's material: a mark needs a picture and the light and shadows of the surface under it, so it is Bevy 0.20's built-in decal material (`ForwardDecalMaterial<StandardMaterial>`: `base_color` and `base_color_texture`, alpha blended, `perceptual_roughness`, `unlit`). One entity per live mark, made as the kind's pool grows (never more than its `max_live`) and hidden when its slot is empty; a material per entity, changed only when its fade moves. Every camera with `AiCamera`, and a first-person camera, gets a `DepthPrepass` while marks are laid or telegraph decals are on (the same extra depth pass the telegraphs already cost).

**Where marks come from.** The game lays one with `shards::fx::spawn_mark(world, "blood_pool", point, normal)` (an error says what is wrong, `spawn_mark_seeded` takes the seed) or `commands.trigger(PlayMark::new("blood_pool", point, normal))`, as with `PlayEffect`. The `fx` table lays them from events: its new map `marks` (event → a list of links, left out of the written form when empty) and, for the effects of the same events, `effects`. A link `(mark, place, count, spread, offset)` finds the surface by `place`:

| event | where it happens | the effect's `aim` and `toward` | `place` can be |
|---|---|---|---|
| `shot_impact` | a pellet stopped at a `WORLD` surface (`ShotImpact` with a `collider`): its point | `Surface`: out along the surface's normal | `At` (the mark lies there, along the normal), `Behind`, `Below` |
| `shot_hit` | a pellet went through a body (`ShotImpact` with a `target`): where it met it | `Hit` back towards the shooter, `Away` on | `Behind`, `Below` |
| `damaged` | a blow landed (an ignored one, `invulnerable`, lays none): the feet of the one hit, with `offset` | as for any hit | `Behind`, `Below` |
| `died` | someone died: their feet | (the effect is the table's `effects.died`) | `Behind` (when a killer is known), `Below` |
| `part_broken` | a body part broke off (`PartBroken`): at the part | `Hit` back towards the attacker, `Away` on | `Behind`, `Below` |

`Behind(reach)` is the nearest `WORLD` surface along the event's direction within `reach` metres, found by a ray from the event's point (plus `offset`): for a shot, the direction the shot flew (the way from where `ShotFired` says it started to where it hit); for a blow, from the attacker to the body, level. `Below(reach)` is the nearest surface straight down. `count` marks per event, each searched in a cone of `spread` degrees across (0 to 180, as an effect's `spread`) round the way, so blood scatters; the seed is the event's (its point, its normal, the pellet), never the simulation's `SimRng`, so a shot lays the same marks on a co-op host and on its clients. A search that finds nothing within `reach` lays nothing; `At` needs no search. **A shot fires both `shot_hit` and `damaged`**: link them to different marks (the splatter on the wall from the shot's own direction, the pool under the body from the blow), never the same one twice. An `effect` gets `Aim::Away` (out of the far side, away from the attacker) and `Aim::Surface` (along the normal), and the events `shot_impact`, `shot_hit` and `part_broken` join `damaged`, `died` and the rest in the table's `effects`.

**Debris: particles that land.** An effect with `collide: true` has particles that are stepped against the world instead of flown by a formula. Each step (1/60 s of the simulation's clock, the same whatever the frame rate: a frame that comes late takes the steps it missed, and a particle ends up where the same steps put it) casts a ray along the way through the physics world's `WORLD` colliders (read-only, a collider on the voxel field too: `PhysicsWorld::raycast`), and the particle meets what the ray meets: it bounces (`restitution`, the share of its speed along the surface it keeps, 0 to 1), loses speed along the surface (`friction`, Coulomb's: it takes `friction × (1 + restitution) × the speed it came in at` off the speed along the surface, and holds a sliding particle back by `friction × gravity`), slides, follows the ground down a step of up to 15 cm, falls off an edge, and comes to rest when it is slower than 0.1 m/s on a surface at most 60° steep, lying on its side with its up along the surface's normal. A bounce slower than 0.6 m/s settles it, and 32 bounces end the bouncing whatever the speed. A ceiling does not hold it: it drops. A particle's size sets how far its middle rests from the surface (half of it). Particles of an effect that lands may also have a `mesh: "models/chunk.glb"` (a glTF: the first primitive of its first mesh, or `"models/chunk.glb#Mesh1/Primitive0"`; drawn at `size` times its own size, so make it about a unit across; shaded as a cube is, or lit by itself with `glow` and `unlit`; the particle's colour; no UVs needed) or an `image: "textures/leaf.png"` (a `Quad` wears a picture: its colour times the picture's, its shape the picture's alpha) in place of its `shape`. These two need no `collide`: any effect may have them.

- `rest: Fade` (the default) — a particle at rest lies there as long as its `lifetime` says and fades as every particle does; the 30 s cap holds. `rest: UntilCleared` — it lies there until it is cleared or the pool recycles it for a newer one; its `lifetime` is then how long it may fly before it lands (a chunk that never lands, falling into the void, is gone at its end as any particle is) and the time it takes to reach its look at the end (`color_end`, `size_end`), which it keeps: give `color_end` the colour it should lie there in.
- The pool's `max_live` is the cap of what lies there: a play that finds the pool full takes the place of the oldest particle, flying or at rest.
- Rays are the cost: one a step in flight, one or two on the ground, none at rest. A frame casts at most `GoreStats::budget` of them (2048); the steps it leaves are taken by the next frame (a `step 600` between two frames is caught up over a few). A particle that lands is never expired before its steps have caught up with the clock, so a late frame does not take a chunk that has come to rest in the time it was not stepped through.
- A particle in free flight (no `collide`) is as it was: a function of its age, through everything; effects that never name the new fields write and read as before, bit for bit (`an_effect_without_the_new_fields_reads_and_writes_as_it_always_did`).

**Clearing.** `shards_fx::clear(world, tag)` takes away the marks of the kinds whose `tags` hold `tag` and the particles (those of the effects whose `tags` hold it, flying or at rest) and says how many (`Cleared { marks, particles }`); `clear_all` takes everything; the tool `fx_clear tag=gore` (or `all=true`) does the same from outside and works headless (it finds nothing). A new world clears everything by itself: `ai_core::WorldRebuilt` (a region change, `regen`, a snapshot load, a client's rebase) and the engine leaving `InGame` for the main menu. A snapshot that sets the clock back removes the marks laid "later", as it does the particles.

**For agents.** `effects` (Dev, query) lists, after the effects, the table's links (`marks on shot_hit: blood_splat Behind(8.0)`), the marks per kind (what and how big, `alive 3/96`) and the debris; `effect_play` plays any effect (`toward` is the normal for an `aim: Surface`); `mark_spawn mark=bullet_hole point=[x,y,z] normal=[x,y,z]` (Dev, control; not recorded in replays) lays a mark, or `from=[x,y,z] toward=[dx,dy,dz] reach=20` finds the surface for you; `fx_clear` takes them away. `ai/status` has `fx: {…, "marks": 3, "debris": {"resting": 5, "flying": 0}, "rays": {"last": 0, "max": 381, "total": 4120, "budget": 2048}}`: the performance counters of the gore (live marks, the debris at rest and in flight, the rays of the last frame, the most in any frame so far and in all). Without a picture `effects` says `3 marks · nothing is drawn headless: marks are laid in a window or with --offscreen`, lists the kinds with `up to N`, has no `debris:` line, and `mark_spawn` refuses (``nothing is drawn headless: marks are laid in a window or with --offscreen (mark `bullet_hole` is known)``); an event lays nothing.

```text
$ shards act mark_spawn mark=bullet_hole from=[0,41.6,0] toward=[0,0,-1]
laid bullet_hole at (0.00, 41.60, -5.75) on a surface facing (0.00, 0.00, 1.00), 0.13 m across: 1/96 alive
$ shards act part id=e25 name=head op=break
$ shards act effects
...
marks on part_broken: blood_splat Behind(8.0)
marks on shot_hit: blood_splat Behind(8.0)
marks on shot_impact: bullet_hole At
3 marks · 5 alive
  blood_pool   spot #5c0b0e · 0.4-0.8 m · until cleared · fade in 1.5 s · tags gore, blood · alive 1/32
  blood_splat  textures/marks/blood_splat.png #7a1014 · 0.25-0.6 m · until cleared · fade in 0.25 s · tags gore, blood · alive 2/64
  bullet_hole  textures/marks/bullet_hole.png #ffffff · 0.1-0.16 m · 120 s · fade out 30 s · tags gore · alive 2/96
debris: 5 at rest, 0 in flight · rays last frame 0, most 381, budget 2048
$ shards act fx_clear tag=gore
cleared 5 marks and 5 particles tagged `gore`
```

**Checking the content.** `--check-content` names the file, the definition and the field. A mark: a size that is not `(min, max)` with `0 < min <= max`, a `fade_in` or `fade_out` below 0, a `fade_out` on an `UntilCleared` mark (nothing to fade towards), fades that do not fit in a `Secs` lifetime, a `Secs` lifetime that is not above 0 or is past a day, `max_live` outside 1…4096, `depth` not above 0, `roughness` outside 0…1, a colour that does not read, a `texture` that is not a `.png`, leaves the assets folder (`..`, a drive, a leading slash) or is no file there, tags that are empty, longer than 64 or repeated. An effect: `restitution` outside 0…1, a negative `friction`, `restitution`, `friction` or `rest` set without `collide: true`, `rest: UntilCleared` with a `gravity` that is not below 0 (it would never come to rest), a `mesh` that is not a `.glb` or `.gltf`, leaves the assets folder or is no file, a `mesh` with a `shape` or an `image`, an `image` with a `shape` other than `Quad`, tags. A link: an event that lays no marks (`marks: no event `shot_imapct` lays marks (did you mean `shot_impact`?)`), an unknown mark (with the closest), a `count` outside 1…16, a `spread` outside 0…180, a reach not above 0 or past 100 m, `At` on an event with no surface of its own (only `shot_impact` has one), `At` with a `count`, `spread` or `offset`.

**Performance.** With no mark and no landing particle nothing is made or cast: `draw_marks` finds no kind, `step_debris` finds no effect that lands, and the depth prepass the cameras already have for the telegraph decals stays as it was. A mark costs its decal's quad (the transparent pass, one draw each: they are not batched, since each has its own material); the debris costs rays (counted above). The `reference` performance scene shows no change with no gore on screen (a debug build, base and F9 run back to back three times each: 267, 268 and 265 frames per second against 270, 269 and 270, a tick of 1.00, 0.98 and 1.00 ms against 0.98, 0.97 and 0.99, GPU 0.63 ms and 83 draws in both; the 378 more entities are the three new effects' hidden pools, 368 meshes, and they are not drawn). Budgets: the live marks are at most the sum of the kinds' `max_live`, the debris at most the effects' `max_live`, the rays at most `GoreStats::budget` a frame; the test `ten_times_the_pool_of_chunks_leaves_the_pool_full_and_the_oldest_recycled` plays ten times the pool and counts.

**Co-op.** `ShotFired`, `ShotImpact`, `Damaged` and `Died` are net events, so a client lays the marks and plays the effects its host's shots, blows and deaths ask for, on its own, as it does the sparks of a hit (and the host's seed is the event's, so the same marks). `PartBroken` is **not** a net event (nothing forwards it today): the chunks and the marks linked to `part_broken` appear on the host and in solo play; a client sees the chunks a `died` link asks for, and the marks and sparks of a shot. A host without a window lays nothing, as a headless machine never does.

**Limits.** Marks are laid in world space: a mark on a door, a lift or any collider that moves stays where it was laid while the surface goes (no parenting yet). Decals on bodies (a mark that sticks to a character) are not built: a mark only paints what is within its `depth` of the plane it was laid on, so a body that stands there is painted at its feet and not above. A decal is a flat quad: it is as good as the surface is flat; on a curved or very steep-viewed surface its edges stretch (a first-person camera that looks along a wall sees a hole smeared). The depth fade makes a mark vanish on a surface more than `depth` away from its plane (a hole on a wall does not wrap round an inside corner unless `depth` is big). Debris sees `WORLD` colliders only, never bodies, and the physics world as the last tick left it (a mover that has just moved is a tick late). The chunks and marks a `shot_hit` sprays are not a ray against the bodies behind the first (`pierce`): only the first world surface along the shot gets the blood.

**Deviations from the spec, on purpose.** (1) The spec's `lifetime` for a mark is `Secs(f32) | UntilCleared`; so is the field. (2) The cap and the pool of resting debris are the effect's `max_live`, not a second number: a pool is one number for what flies and what lies. (3) `fade_out` is an error for an `UntilCleared` mark instead of a silent nothing. (4) The shot's direction is not on `ShotImpact` (F3's event is as F3 left it): the picture remembers where each shooter's last `ShotFired` started and takes the way from there to the point (the way back along the normal when it has not seen one). (5) Marks need no new `Intent`, `AiId` or net event: they ride the ones that exist.

## Lights and colour grading (F13)

A light is content, and so is the colour of the picture. The `shards_light` module turns `light` definitions (`*.light.ron`) into the Bevy lights a picture draws; the camera's picture (`picture.grading`, `shards_motion`) carries a colour grade that trigger volumes in a level can change. Both are only pictures: nothing in a tick reads them, so a replay never diverges over them, and a mistake in one is found by `--check-content`. What a snapshot holds is the placed `ContentLight` and `GradingVolume` components with their entities, like any reflected component; the lights' state (`LightState`) and the grade's blend (`GradingBlend`) are presentation state: neither changes the simulation or a replay's checks, `GradingBlend` is moved by each tick's volumes (`FixedLast`) and both are worked out again from the clock after a snapshot loads.

![the lit sandbox room at dusk: a flashing lamp on and off (top), and the player left of the grading volume's line and inside it (bottom)](media/lights.png)

```ron
// content/light/lights.light.ron
{
    "lamp": (color: "#ffe6bf", intensity: 150000.0, range: 12.0, shadows: true),
    "sodium": (color: "#ffb347", intensity: 120000.0, range: 14.0, shadows: true, flicker: Noise(rate: 6.0, depth: 0.25)),
    "tube": (kelvin: 6500.0, intensity: 80000.0, flicker: Pattern(pattern: "mmamammmmammamamaaamammma", rate: 10.0)),
    "torch": (kind: Spot(inner_deg: 25.0, outer_deg: 50.0), intensity: 300000.0, range: 20.0, shadows: true),
}
// content/light/grading.grading.ron
{ "rust": (blend_s: 1.5, grading: (temperature: 0.1, tint: 0.05, saturation: 0.8, contrast: 1.1)) }
```

| field of a `light` | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` | `Point` | `Point`, or `Spot(inner_deg, outer_deg)`: a cone along the light's own -Z (the way a glTF lamp points), the angles its whole opening in degrees as Blender's *Spot Size* is; `0 < inner_deg <= outer_deg < 180` |
| `color` / `kelvin` | white | the colour as `#rrggbb` (sRGB), or as a temperature from 1000 to 40000 K (1900 a candle, 2700 a bulb, 6500 daylight). Not both |
| `intensity` | `100000` | the power in lumens, as Bevy takes it (`PointLight::intensity`), 0 or more. At Bevy's default camera exposure 20000 is a dim bulb, 100000 a lamp that lights a room, 1000000 a floodlight. A flicker multiplies it |
| `range` | `15` | how far it reaches (m), above 0 and at most 1000 |
| `radius` | `0` | the size of the source (m): bigger softens its highlight |
| `shadows` | `false` | whether it asks for a shadow; the shadow budget decides whether it gets one |
| `flicker` | `None` | `Pattern(pattern, rate)`: one letter `a`-`z` per step, `rate` steps a second, looping; `a` is dark, `m` the light as written, `z` about twice (`(letter - 'a') / 12`), the classic light styles. `Noise(rate, depth)`: smooth noise that wanders between `1 - depth` and 1 times the intensity, `rate` times a second |

The content check names the file, the definition and the field: `intensity` 0 or more, `range` above 0, the spot angles as above, a pattern of the letters `a`-`z` only (and not empty), `rate` above 0 (at most 240), `depth` from 0 to 1, a `color` that reads, a `kelvin` from 1000 to 40000, and not a `color` with a `kelvin`. A `grading` definition (`blend_s`, `grading`) is checked the same way: `blend_s` from 0 to 60 seconds, `temperature` and `tint` from -1 to 1, `exposure` from -10 to 10, `hue_deg` from -180 to 180, `saturation` and `contrast` from 0 to 4, `lift` from -1 to 1, `gamma` from 0.05 to 4, `gain` from 0 to 8. Both kinds are not simulation content (`SIMULATION = false`): editing them never makes a replay diverge.

**Placing a light.** The component `ContentLight { id }` on an entity makes it shine by the definition `id`, from where its `Transform` is (a spot along its -Z): a level node with the property `light = "sodium"` (the table in "Levels from Blender": a Blender lamp, or an empty), a prefab (`"ContentLight": (id: "lamp")`), or code (`commands.spawn((ContentLight::new("lamp"), Transform::from_xyz(2.0, 3.0, 0.0)))`). **On a Blender lamp, `light=` replaces the lamp's light:** the glTF loader's own `PointLight` or `SpotLight` under that node is taken out of the picture and the content light stands at the node, so the file keeps a lamp for Blender's viewport and the game keeps the numbers in content. A game's other Bevy lights (a sun, a lamp with no `light=`) are the game's and are left alone. The node's name and place are the light's identity (the tie-break of the shadow budget and the noise's seed). The entity that carries `ContentLight` has no `AiId` unless a prefab gives it an `AiKind`; the Bevy light is a child of it (`LightPicture`), so headless and drawn games have the same components on the entities that count. `ContentLight` and `GradingVolume` are `replay_ignore`d (a trigger marker has an id, and so may a lamp prefab), so a replay's hash never sees them; snapshots still hold them.

**Flicker is the simulation's clock.** The brightness at a moment is a pure function of `Time<Fixed>` (elapsed plus the overstep between ticks) and of a seed that is the light's own (its definition's id, its node name and its place when it first appeared; `LightSeeds` keeps it while the light is placed, so a lamp that is carried about wanders as it did, at the rate its definition and `accessibility.flashes` allow), never `SimRng`: a pause freezes a flicker, `step 30` moves it half a second, a headless game and a drawn one show the same brightness at the same tick, and a test knows the letter at tick 30. A pattern with one letter (`"g"`) is a steady brightness (`g` is 6/12: half), which is how a test names one. Two lamps with one noise definition wander differently, and the same lamp does the same in every run. **The player's `accessibility.flashes`** shapes every flicker as it does the attack warnings, since a light that flickers is what a photosensitive player asks to be spared: `full` is as written; `reduced` is no faster than twice a second (`flicker::REDUCED_RATE`) and half as far from the light as written (a noise's depth halved, a pattern's dark letters half light); `off` is steady. The `lights` query says which is in force and shows the flicker as drawn.

**The shadow budget.** `graphics.shadow_lights` (default 4, 0 to 64, `settings_set group=graphics key=shadow_lights value=2`; `graphics.shadows = "off"` is none) says how many content lights may cast a shadow at once. Of the lights whose definition says `shadows: true`, the ones nearest the viewer get one; the viewer is the active camera (the AI's `AiCamera`, else a `ThirdPersonCamera` or a `FirstPersonCamera`), and a game with no camera (headless) measures from the local player's eye; with no camera and no local player there is no viewer, the `lights` query says so and every distance is unknown, and ties go by the key alone. Distances are compared to the centimetre and ties go by a key made of the definition's id, the node's name and the place, never by `Entity`, so a shot taken twice from one place shows the same shadows and a headless game agrees with a drawn one standing there. There is no hysteresis: a light that comes nearer than one that has a shadow takes it, once. A cube shadow map is six passes, so this is the knob for a weak GPU. Only content lights that ask are counted: a game's own Bevy lights keep their own `shadow_maps_enabled`.

**Colour grading.** `picture.grading` of the `camera` content is a `Grading`: `exposure` (stops), `temperature` and `tint` (white balance: positive is redder or more magenta), `hue_deg`, `saturation`, `contrast`, `lift`, `gamma`, `gain` (the offset, power and slope of the ASC CDL). It becomes Bevy's `ColorGrading` on every 3D camera with a `ThirdPersonCamera` or a `FirstPersonCamera` (the same cameras as the rest of the picture), the same values for the shadows, the midtones and the highlights; Bevy grades just before tone mapping, so a camera whose `tone_mapping` is `None` shows none of it. Per-channel lift/gamma/gain wheels and a LUT are not in Bevy's built-in path (its sections are scalar, its LUT is the tone mapper's), so they are not here: `temperature` and `tint` are the colour casts. A camera keeps its own `ColorGrading` (a game's) while the content says nothing, and gets it back when the content stops saying anything.

A **grading volume** changes it where the player stands. A level node with `marker = "trigger"` (a collider shapes it, `auto` by default) and `grading = "rust"`, or a prefab with `"GradingVolume": (id: "rust")` on an entity with a trigger `Volume`: while the local player's body touches it (`MotionState::volumes`), the picture blends from what it shows toward the `rust` definition over its `blend_s` (eased, smoothstep), holds it, and blends back to the camera's own grade over the same time when the player leaves; a game with no local player uses the volumes the camera stands in. Where volumes overlap, the one placed last (the highest collider id) wins; a blend that changes course starts from what is shown, so nothing jumps. The state is the resource `GradingBlend`, tracked in `FixedLast` on every tick (so a `step` of 100 ticks sees the tick the player crossed the line) and evaluated on the simulation's clock, which is why a headless game can say where the blend is. It is in no snapshot or replay.

**For the AI.** The query `lights` (player scope, the same headless and drawn): the lights by kind, how many flicker, how many want a shadow and cast one against the budget, the viewer the budget measures from, and a line per light: its definition, name, place, distance, lumens now against its definition's, the flicker (pattern step and letter, or noise, with the percentage now) and `shadow: yes`, `no (over the budget)`, `no (budget 0)` or `not asked`; then the grade the picture shows and where its blend is (the line reads "blending toward `rust`, 62 % done", "holding `rust` (blend done)", "blending back to the camera's own, 30 % done" or "the camera's own"). `lights id=sodium` lists one definition, `limit=` the first lights (24). `ai/status` has `light: {lights, casting, flickering, budget}`. The tool refreshes the state first, as a frame does, so a stepped game answers for now.

```text
$ shards act lights
lights: 6 (point 5, spot 1) · 4 flicker · 3 want a shadow, 3 cast one (budget 4: graphics.shadow_lights) · clock 1.500 s
viewer: the camera at (111.2, -4.6, 9.0)
  dimmer "Lamp.Dim" point at (117.0, -7.0, 2.0) 9.4 m away · 50000 lm of 100000 · pattern `g` at 1/s, step 0 = g: 50 % (50000 lm) · shadow: not asked
  flasher "Lamp.Flash" point at (112.0, -7.0, -4.0) 13.3 m away · 0 lm of 400000 · pattern `ma` at 1/s, step 1 = a: 0 % (0 lm) · shadow: not asked
  lamp "Lamp.Steady" point at (109.0, -7.0, 0.0) 9.6 m away · 150000 lm of 150000 · steady · shadow: yes
  sodium "Lamp.Sodium" point at (107.0, -7.0, -2.0) 12.0 m away · 98740 lm of 120000 · noise 6/s depth 0.25: 82 % (98740 lm) · shadow: yes
  …
grading: the camera's own
  shows: no grade of the content (the camera keeps whatever the game gave it)
  the target has changed 0 times
```

**In the sandbox.** `content/light/` has the lights (`lamp`, `sodium`, `tube`, `flasher`, `dimmer`, `torch`), the gradings (`rust`, `cold`), the prefabs `lit_lamp` and `lit_flasher`, and the level `lit_room` (`assets/levels/lit_room.gltf`, written by `tests/sandbox/lights.rs`): a floor and three walls with six lights (four on Blender lamps that the content lights replace, two on empties) and a trigger volume over its right half that grades with `rust`. `scenarios/lights.scenario` plays it with queries alone, so it runs headless. Tests: `shards_light` (unit tests for the definitions, the flicker and the budget; `tests/light/` for the content check, the query, the clock and the Bevy lights of a drawn game) and the sandbox's `lights.rs`, whose `#[ignore]`d tests need a GPU (`cargo test -p sandbox --test sandbox -- --ignored lights`): the picture holds exactly the six content lights, a flashing lamp lights the room at one moment and not at the next, and a grading volume changes the channel means of the shot and gives them back.

**What is not here.** Directional lights (a sun) are not content yet. Emissive bulbs do not follow a flicker (the material is the game's). There is no area light or light cookie, no hysteresis in the budget, and a spot's shadow costs one pass where a point light's costs six, which the budget does not tell apart. The view model's camera (F1b) takes the world camera's grade when that camera does not draw in HDR; under an HDR camera (any `picture.bloom`) it draws over the graded picture and stays ungraded, and any other second camera that draws the world is the game's to grade. Checked on a GPU with `--offscreen` (RTX 5080); not checked by eye in a window.

## Hit stop (C2)

When a blow lands, the picture stands still for a beat (60-100 ms). It is what makes a hit feel heavy, and it is a **hold, never slow motion**: the simulation does not pass at a fraction of its speed, and no tick is lost or added. `shards_hitstop` turns the combat events into holds by a table in content, and each machine does with a hold what suits it: alone with a picture it keeps the real-time clock still, in co-op it holds only the pictures of the bodies in the blow (a headless co-op host or client records those holds too, though nothing draws them), and a headless game alone, a stepped one and a replay hold nothing at all.

```ron
// crates/sandbox/assets/content/fx/sandbox.hitstop.ron (abbreviated)
{
    "sandbox": (
        max_seconds: 0.12,
        cooldown: 0.0,
        rules: [
            (name: "finisher", when: (event: Damaged, weight_at_least: Finisher), seconds: 0.10),
            (name: "poise break", when: (event: Damaged, weight_at_least: Break), seconds: 0.10),
            (name: "counter", when: (event: Damaged, weight_at_least: Counter), seconds: 0.08),
            (name: "heavy hit", when: (event: Damaged, reaction_at_least: 2), seconds: 0.08),
            (name: "hit", when: (event: Damaged), seconds: 0.06),
            (name: "block", when: (event: Blocked), seconds: 0.06),
            (name: "parry", when: (event: Parried), seconds: 0.10),
            (name: "perfect dodge", when: (event: PerfectEvaded, solo: true), seconds: 0.10),
        ],
    ),
}
```

**The table (kind `hitstop`, `*.hitstop.ron`, one per game, not simulation content).** The engine has no names from any game: the ladder of a game (which blow holds how long) is its own content, and the sandbox's is a neutral example. `rules` are tried in order and **the first rule that matches an event gives the hold**; an event no rule matches gives none. A rule has an optional `name` (the journal and the tools show it; else `rule 3 damaged`), `when` and `seconds`. `when` asks, all of it at once, of the combat event:

| field | the event has it | matches |
|---|---|---|
| `event` | always | `Damaged`, `Blocked`, `Parried`, `PerfectEvaded`, `GuardBroken`, `Staggered` (left out: any event) |
| `weight_at_least` | `Damaged`, `Blocked`, `GuardBroken` | the hit's `HitWeight` is at least this: `Light < Heavy < Counter < Break < Finisher` (the engine raises it to `Heavy` for a reaction of tier 2 or 3 and to `Break` for a poise the blow really breaks: a blow that kills breaks nothing, so it keeps the weight it would have without the break, as the corpse takes no poise and no `Staggered` follows; with a game's lethal hook (B5) the answer decides: a blow it lays down is weighed as a kill, one it lets the body survive keeps its break; a game's hook sets `Counter` and `Finisher`) |
| `reaction_at_least` | `Damaged` | the reaction tier the hit asks of its target |
| `cause` | `Staggered` | `PoiseBroken`, `Parried`, `GuardBroken`, `Dev` |
| `action` | all but `Staggered` | the id of the action that hit |
| `ignored` | `Damaged` | by default a rule matches only a hit that landed; `ignored: true` matches one that was ignored (god mode, i-frames) |
| `involves_local` | all | `true`: only a blow the local player is in (attacker, target or defender) matches; a fight between two others, a hazard tick or a crowd far away then holds nothing. Put it on the rules of a game that should never stutter for the fights around the player (the sandbox does); the setting `hit_stop_local_only` does the same for every rule |
| `solo` | all | `true`: only a machine that is **not in a co-op session** (`NetRole::Single`) matches. Hosting counts as co-op even before anyone has joined, and so does being a client: such a machine holds the pictures of the bodies and never the clock, and a picture hold in co-op is still a hold, so a rule for solo play only is how a game gives a hold to solo and none online (or, with a second rule after it, a shorter one). Off by default, and left out of the file at its default (a rule without it hashes as before; writing `solo: true` changes the content hash like any edit to a definition, so a co-op host and its clients need the same file). The sandbox's perfect dodge uses it. `hitstop_play` names the case when a rule is passed over for being solo-only. A rule with `solo` is shadowed by an earlier rule without it, not the other way round (the content check names that) |

So "finisher, then poise break, then counter, then a heavy reaction, then the rest" is five rules in that order, and a game that wants a different order writes it. `max_seconds` (at most 0.5 s, the engine's own ceiling) bounds every hold whatever a rule says, and `cooldown` (s) keeps a flurry of hits from turning into a stutter: a hold does not start within that time after the last one ended. Holds that overlap **merge by the later end**: a hold asked for while one runs lasts as long as the longer of the two has left. The content check names what cannot work: a second table, a rule longer than `max_seconds`, a rule the ones before it cover (it can never match), a `weight_at_least` on a parry (it has no weight), a `reaction_at_least` or a `cause` on the wrong event.

**What a machine does with a hold.** Every machine that sees the combat events (it simulates them, or it is a co-op client whose host forwards them) triggers `HitStopped { event, rule, name, seconds, bodies, ids }` and writes `hitstop: finisher 0.10 s (damaged) on e5, e6` to the journal as a `local` line (it is this machine's own, never sent to another and never a gameplay event). The observer changes nothing in the world, so it needs no `simulates` guard. Then:

| machine | the hold |
|---|---|
| alone (`NetRole::Single`), a window or `--offscreen`, in real time | the **clock hold** (`ai_core::ClockHold`): the virtual clock's relative speed is forced to 0 for the real time of the hold (not a pause: no pause menu, no muted sound, the gate does not refuse). `Time<Fixed>` gathers nothing, so no tick is due and none is added when it ends; everything on the simulation's clock stands still, the pose and the particles with it; the camera and the input run on real time. A hold lasts its time plus less than a frame. `speed` still reports the player's speed, and a `speed` call during a hold changes what the clock comes back to |
| a co-op host or client | **no clock hold at all**: the picture of each body in the blow stands still (`ai_core::PresentationHolds`, by `AiId`): the animation bridge pauses the body's `AnimationPlayer` and switches nothing until it ends, and the body's whole drawn pose (position and rotation, on the visual child; for a client's remote body in `shards_net`'s interpolation) stays where it was when the hold began, then blends linearly to the live drawn pose over as long as the hold lasted, so a held 0.1 s catches up over 0.1 s without a snap; no `Transform` of an `AiId` entity is touched. A client decides for itself from the combat events its host forwards; a headless host or stand records the same holds, and nothing draws them |
| alone, and headless, `--paused`, a `step` (it ends a hold that runs), a replay playing back (`--verify`, also with `--windowed`), a driven clock, a paused clock, a loading gate | nothing is held (a co-op host or client, headless or in a stand, still holds the pictures as the row above says). The event and the journal line are still there, and `hitstop` says why nothing was held |

A hold is never part of the simulation: `ClockHold` and `PresentationHolds` are not in snapshots or replays, the `hitstop` kind is outside the replay's content hash, and a replay recorded with the clock held verifies identical with hit stop off, headless and in a window that plays it (a test in `crates/sandbox/tests/sandbox/hitstop.rs`).

**The player's settings** (`settings`, group `accessibility`): `hit_stop` is the scale of every hold, 0 to 1 (0 turns hit stop off; the sandbox's settings menu has a slider), and `hit_stop_local_only` holds only for the blows the local player (`LocalPlayer`) is in, not for the fights around them.

**For agents.** `hitstop` (Dev, query; `last=N` lists the last N holds) shows how this machine holds, the settings, the table with each rule's hold, whether the clock is held now (and for how much longer, and the speed it reads), the pictures held, the totals and, for the clock, the real time it held in all and **the ticks that ran inside a hold (0 when it works)**. `hitstop_play` (Dev, control; not recorded in replays) makes a hold as a blow would: `event=damaged weight=Break attacker=e5 target=e6`, or `seconds=0.08` to skip the table; it answers the rule and what this machine did with it. `ai/status` has `hitstop: {mode, rules, events, clock_holds, picture_holds, skipped, clock_held_ms, ticks_inside, clock_held_now}`, and the developer menu has `hitstop` under combat.

```
$ shards act hitstop_play event=damaged weight=Break attacker=e5 target=e6
poise break 0.10 s (damaged): clock held (0.10 s)
$ shards act hitstop
hit stop: solo: holds the real-time clock (no tick is lost)
...
clock: 0.117 s held in all over 1 holds · ticks that ran inside a hold: 0 · the last: 0.117 s real, 0 ticks inside
```

**Limits.** In co-op the pose of the bodies in the blow stands still (animation and drawn position); what the pictures do on their own clocks (camera, UI) run on. The held time is the time asked for plus up to about two frames: it starts from the start of the frame in which the blow is seen and is checked at the start of each frame (a measured 0.5 s hold took 0.51 s). The `Time<Virtual>` of a held clock is 0, so presentation that runs on it (a particle's life, `Res<Time>` in `Update`) stands still with the world; what must not stand still reads `Time<Real>`.

**Deviations from the design, on purpose.** (1) The co-op picture hold freezes the whole drawn pose, not only the animation (the lead's answer to the first open question): `PresentationHolds::drawn` is asked by the one rule's two places, `shards_motion::interp::blend` (local and predicted bodies, the follow camera then follows the held picture) and `shards_net::interp::show` (a client's remote bodies); the catch-up is linear over the hold's length, like the interpolation blend itself. (2) The hold's systems are unnamed `First` systems in `ai_core` and the plugin has no `SystemSet` of its own: nothing orders against them, the hold is not simulation. (3) No reference replay is recorded with hit stop on: a hold changes no tick, so a recording is the same file with or without it; the test in `crates/sandbox/tests/sandbox/hitstop.rs` records one while the clock is held and verifies it with hit stop off, headless and in a window. (4) `hitstop_play seconds=` keeps the table's `max_seconds` and is journalled as `manual`.

## Rules (C3)

A world plays one **rule set** at a time (a mode; the examples here are `gentle`, `plain` and `harsh`), and the rule set says how the engine's numbers change for each **class** of body: the health damage a body takes and the damage it deals, its maximum health and poise, the stamina its actions cost, its guards' perfect window, the max of its named charges; and, for every director, the attack tokens and the rest after an attack. A **session table** scales a class by the number of players in the session. The host decides, and only out of combat. `shards_rules` (slice C3.1a) holds the content, the state, the reads, the guards and the tools; slice C3.1b wires it to the rest of the engine (the NPC module's guard, the world save section, the `rules.*` UI sources, the net event and the net session filter, see "Wiring" below); the hook sites that read the rules come with the slices: damage (C3.2, below) and stamina (C3.4a, below) are built; the maxima, the perfect window, charges, tokens and rest (C3.3, C3.4b, C3.5) are not. Until a slice lands, its numbers in a rule set change what `rules` says, the session count and what a save keeps, and nothing a body does.

```ron
// content/rules/game.rules.ron
{
    "default": (
        modes: ["gentle", "plain", "harsh"],
        start: "plain",
        classes: ["brute"],
        session: {"brute": (max_health: [1.0, 1.5])},
        blocked: "@rules-blocked",
        host_only: "@rules-host-only",
    ),
}
// content/rules/modes.rule_set.ron (abbreviated)
{
    "harsh": (
        name: "@rules-harsh",
        summary: "@rules-harsh-summary",
        classes: {
            "player": (incoming_damage: 1.5, charges: {"flask": 2}),
            "brute": (max_health: 1.5),
        },
        attack_tokens: (shift: 1),
        attack_rest: 0.5,
    ),
}
```

**Content.** Two kinds, both simulation content:

| kind | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `rules` (`*.rules.ron`, `RulesDef`) | the one definition `default`: `modes` (the rule sets in the order a menu lists them and `cycle` steps through them), `start` (the rule set a new world starts with, never the previous world's), `classes` (the classes a rule set, a session row and a `RuleClass` may name; `player` is always one), `session` (factors by session size, by class and column `max_health`, `max_poise`, `outgoing_damage`: entry n − 1 is for n players, more players than entries take the last), `blocked` (what a player reads when a guard refuses a change) and `host_only` (what a co-op guest reads: the host chooses) |
| `rule_set` (`*.rule_set.ron`, `RuleSetDef`) | one definition per mode: `name` and `summary` (Fluent ids), `classes` (by class: `incoming_damage`, `outgoing_damage`, `max_health`, `max_poise` as factors, `stamina_cost` as rules of `tags` and a `factor`, `perfect_bonus` in seconds, `charges` as the max of named charges), `attack_tokens` (`shift` added to a director's limit, at least `min`; a limit of 0 stays 0) and `attack_rest` (× the rest an NPC takes after an attack it finished). A class it does not name, and every field left out, keep the engine's numbers |

**A game without `rules/default` has no rules:** nothing is inserted into the world, every read returns the engine's numbers, and its replays and snapshots keep their bytes (the sandbox has no rules content, and its fourteen reference replays and the template's two verify identical with the module in).

**The checks** (`--check-content`, a hot edit). A rule set needs `rules/default` and a place in its `modes` (``rule set `x` is not in `rules/default` `modes`: add it there or delete it``), a name, classes the rules know (``class `brut` is not one of `rules/default` `classes` (did you mean `brute`?): player, brute``), every factor above 0 and at most 10 (`` `max_health` 0 of class `brute`: a factor is above 0 and at most 10 (1 changes nothing) ``), a bonus from 0 to 1 s, cost rules with tags, none of them empty and no tag in two rules of a class (`merge them`), charge maxima from 1 to 255 and names of 1 to 64 characters without control characters, a token shift from −8 to 8 and a `min` from 0 to 64, and no `min` without a shift (`` `attack_tokens.min` 2 without a `shift` changes nothing: give a shift or leave `min` out ``). The rules are one definition, `default` (``the rules are one definition, `default`; `x` would be a second``), with `modes` not empty, without repeats, each an existing rule set, `start` among them, `classes` of lowercase letters, digits and `_` without repeats, session rows of known classes, each giving at least one column (``` `session.brute` gives no column: give `max_health`, `max_poise` or `outgoing_damage`, or remove the row ```) of at most 8 entries of factors, `blocked` and `host_only` Fluent texts that exist, and every rule set setting the same charges for a class (``class `player`: charge `flask` is set by `gentle` but not by `plain`: every rule set sets the same charges``). A prefab's `RuleClass` reads as a class (`("brute")`; without a type registry, as in a bare check of the folder, the check `rule_class` says a value that does not read) and names a class of `rules/default` (``RuleClass `brut` is not a class of `rules/default` (did you mean `brute`?): player, brute``). A `RuleClass` a level file gives a node is not checked yet: nothing reads a class until the bodies are brought to the rules (C3.3a).

**The state.**

| item | what it is | snapshot, replay, net |
|---|---|---|
| `ActiveRules { mode, generation, players }` (resource) | the rule set in play (empty: neutral, every read gives the engine's numbers), a generation that counts changes of what the rules say (a mode change, a content change), and the session size bodies are scaled for | `add_snapshot_resource` and the prepare `rules`; the optional replay check `rules` hashes the three while the resource exists and is not neutral (neutral = absent); replicated, never removed in a session with peers |
| `RuleClass("brute")` (component) | the class the rules know a body by, authored in prefabs (`"RuleClass": ("brute")`); a body with `PlayerId` and no class is `player`, a body with neither is untouched | with its body |
| `RuleScaled` (component) | what the rules did to a body: the key of its last apply, the bases of its maximum health and poise, the charges a change still owes; the type is here, its writer (`shards_action::rules_apply`) comes with C3.3a, the charges it owes with C3.3b | with its body |
| `SessionFilter` (resource, set at build time) | which bodies with `PlayerId` count toward the session size; the default seats every body, and the umbrella's net wiring leaves out a body that waits for its player's rejoin (`NetLeft`) | not saved, not sent |
| `RulesGuards` (resource, registered at build time) | what a change of rules must wait for: `app.add_rules_guard(name, fn(&World) -> Option<String>)`, asked in order, the first reason wins (`… [name]`); the NPC module registers `npc_engaged` (below), a game adds its own | not saved, not sent |

**When it changes.**
- **A new world** (`OnEnter(InGame)`, `start_rules` in the set `RulesSystems::Start`) plays `start`: the resource is inserted (or a neutral one overwritten, its generation + 1, no players counted yet) and the journal says ``rules: a new world plays `plain` ``. It triggers no event: a new world shows no banner. Nothing on a co-op client (the host's resource replicates) or without `rules/default`. A region trip hides `OnEnter` and `OnExit` of `InGame`, so the world keeps its mode across regions. A game's `OnEnter(InGame)` system that must see the new world's rules goes `.after(RulesSystems::Start)`. The module's system changed the order Bevy sorts unordered `OnEnter(InGame)` systems in: a game with two or more spawn systems there orders them itself, or their bodies may get other `AiId`s than before and its replays diverge.
- **The main menu** (`OnExit(InGame)`, `end_rules`): a co-op host sets the resource neutral (a removal does not travel to its clients); alone (no `NetRole`, or `Single`) it is removed, and so is a co-op client's copy of the host's (it is not the client's to write, and it must not block a later world of the client's own). The next world starts at `start`, never at the previous world's mode.
- **A content change** (`on_content_applied`, inside the call that changes content, so a replay runs it at the same tick; nothing on a client). Rules in play add 1 to `generation`, so every body is brought to the new numbers at the next tick. A mode content no longer has, or no longer lists in `modes`, falls back to `start` (neutral if `rules/default` is gone too), with the warning ``rules: the rule set `harsh` is gone from content: playing `plain` `` and `RulesChanged { cause: Content }`. Rules content that appears in a world without rules in play starts them, as a new world would. The call's answer has the line `rules: content changed; bodies are brought to it at the next tick`.
- **A snapshot load** (the prepare `rules`, after the prepare `content`): the world's `ActiveRules` becomes what the snapshot holds; a snapshot without one removes it (a co-op host sets it neutral, since a removal does not travel). A load refused after the prepares ran puts back what the world had.
- **Each tick**, in `SimSet::Input` before the engine's other sets there (`RulesSystems::Apply`, before `WorldSystems::Zones` and `CoreSystems::FollowOrders`, so before every engine set that follows them; on the host and alone only, while `ActiveRules` exists), `count_session` counts the distinct `PlayerId` values among the bodies `SessionFilter` seats (a corpse that keeps its `PlayerId` beside the player's new body counts once; dead and downed players count) and writes the count into `players`. When it moves and the rules' session table gives a factor, the journal says `rules: 2 players: brute health ×1.5`. A game's own `SimSet::Input` systems are not ordered against the set: one that reads the rules (a gate that reads a charge's max, from C3.3b on) goes `.after(RulesSystems::Apply)`.
- **`rules_set`** (below).

`RulesChanged { from, to, cause }` (`cause`: `Call`, `Load`, `Content`) says the rules in play changed; the journal has `rules: plain → harsh (call)` (and `(save)` for a save's world section); the fall back of a content change is said by its warning. On a co-op host the event is sent to the guests (`net_event::<RulesChanged>()`, registered by the umbrella's net wiring, since `shards_rules` does not see `shards_net`), so a guest's HUD shows the banner and its journal has the same line.

**Wiring (C3.1b).**
- **The guard `npc_engaged`** (registered by the NPC module): the rules change only out of combat, and an NPC that fights is combat, a partner's fight too. It holds while an active NPC with a target is in a state of a fighting kind (`chase`, `attack`, `wait_token`; the same test as the condition `npc_engaged`, now one function, `shards::npc::ai::engaged_npc`, which names the first such NPC in `AiId` order). The reason reads ``e6 `skeleton` is fighting (`chase`, target e5) [npc_engaged]`` (the NPC's behaviour in backquotes). A state of another kind (`hold`, `return_home`, a calm one) does not hold the rules. A game adds its own guard with `app.add_rules_guard("name", fn)`.
- **The world section `rules`** (`shards::save_sections::RulesSave`, version 1, registered after `region`): `{"mode": "harsh"}`, or `{"mode": null}` where the game has no rules or none in play. It is written in every game's world saves. Applying `null` (or a file written before the section existed) does nothing at all: no write, no `generation` change, no event, no journal line. A saved mode that is not the one in play sets it, adds 1 to `generation` and triggers `RulesChanged { cause: Load }` (journal ``rules: plain → harsh (save)``); the bodies are brought to it by the next tick, never by the load. A saved mode this game's content does not have (also in a game with no rules at all) is not refused: the journal warns ``rules: the save's rule set `x` is not in this game's content: playing `plain` `` and the mode in play stays. A mode that is longer than 64 bytes or has a control character fails validation: the load is refused before anything is applied (this is a refusal, not file damage, so no backup is tried). Content keeps to the same limit: a rule set id longer than 64 bytes (`shards_rules::MAX_MODE`) is a content error, and ids cannot hold control characters at all, so a game's own rule set can always be saved. A new world plays `start` first, so `continue_game` ends at the saved mode, and a save written before the section existed leaves a continued world at `start`. Nothing on a co-op client. The world slot holds the mode and the character slot never does; the engine never saves on its own when the rules change.
- **The UI sources** (`UiValue::Text`, all read through `peek`): `rules.mode` (the id in play, none without rules), `rules.name` and `rules.summary` (the active rule set's, resolved from Fluent; `rules.name:gentle` is that set's, for a menu that lists the `modes`; none when the text is empty or the rule set does not exist), and `rules.blocked` (on a co-op client the `host_only` text, while a guard holds the `blocked` text, otherwise none).
- **`--difficulty=<id>`** is a game's flag, not the engine's: the game parses it and calls `rules_set mode=<id> force=true` as the agent `cli` (a dev session by default, so `force` is allowed in every build), after `start_rules` and after a `continue_game` load, so the call is recorded after the recording restarts. An id the call refuses is a warning, and the saved mode stays.
- **The prelude** has `RuleClass`.

**For agents.**
- **`rules`** (Player, query; `mode=gentle` describes that rule set instead, without session factors): the mode described, `playing` (the mode in play, whatever `mode` asked about; `null` without rules in play), its name and summary (resolved), `modes`, `start`, the session size, the generation, by class only what differs from the engine's numbers (where a session row scales a factor, the mode's, the session's and their product), the attack tokens and the rest, whether a change is allowed now (`allowed now`, `refused now: … [guard]`, `refused now: a region is loading …`, on a client `the host chooses`) and who decides (by role: `host` on a co-op host, with or without peers yet, and on its clients; `this machine` alone). In a game without rules: ``this game has no rules: add `content/**/*.rules.ron` with the definition `default` and a `*.rule_set.ron` for each mode it lists``.
- **`rules_set`** (Player, action; host only: on a co-op guest the route refuses it before it runs, with ``` `rules_set` runs on the host only: the host chooses the rules: call it on the host (<host>) ```, and the tool refuses a client by itself the same way where no forwarder is set): `mode=harsh`, or `cycle=1` / `cycle=-1` (the next or the one before in `modes`, wrapping around). It refuses, in this order: on a client, outside a world (while a region loads: ``a region is loading: the rules change in the game; call it again once `ai/status` says `engine.state` `InGame` ``), without rules, with both or neither of `mode` and `cycle`, with a `cycle` other than 1 or -1, with an unknown mode (with the closest), with `force=true` from a player's session, and while a guard holds (``the rules change only out of combat: <reason> [npc_engaged]. Wait with `step --until named:rules_changeable`, or pass `force: true` from a dev session``). A refusal records nothing in the replay. The same mode changes nothing (``rules: `plain` already; nothing changed``); another sets the mode, adds 1 to `generation`, triggers `RulesChanged { cause: Call }` and answers `rules: plain → harsh at tick 1834: bodies are brought to it at the start of the next tick; player: incoming damage ×1.5, charge flask 2; brute: health ×1.5; attack tokens +1 (at least 1); attack rest ×0.5`.
- The condition **`rules_changeable`** (rules in play and no guard holds: `step --until named:rules_changeable`), **`ai/status`** → `rules: "gentle · session 2 · generation 4"` (or `"none"`), the engine rule **`rules.mode_known`** (see "Invariants (E11)"), and the developer menu's "Next rule set" (`rules_set cycle=1 force=true`) in its `rules` section; in a game without rules, and on a client, the menu says why it does nothing (`(not here: this game has no rules: …)`).

**Reading the rules** (`shards::rules::read`, for the hook sites and a game's own code): `class_of`, `rules_def`, `active_set`, `class_rules`, `session_size` (and `count_seated` with a query state the caller keeps, as `count_session` does), `session_factor`, `incoming`, `outgoing` (the class's factor × the session row's; a game that captures a body's power for later damage multiplies by it where it captures it), `health_factor`, `poise_factor`, `RulesView::{of, of_entity, stamina_factor, perfect_bonus}` (a body's view of the set in play: none without a set or a class), `charge_rules`, `token_limit`, `rest_factor`. Every one returns the neutral value when there are no rules. The ones that take the content database read through `get`, so what they read counts for the replay check `content`; the tools, the status, the condition and the engine rule read through `peek` and never count.

**Damage (C3.2).** Two factors, read where a hit is made, and neither is cached.

- **Incoming** (the target's class, `incoming_damage`) is multiplied into `DamageCtx::damage` in `modifiers`, right after the `DamageTaken` stage and before `Armor`, and is kept in the new field `DamageCtx::rules` (1 without rules). A hit, a block's chip and a guard break take it; god mode, an evade and a parry return earlier and do not. It does not scale poise, and it does not scale a block's stamina cost (that is set before it). An `Armor` with a flat part takes the flat part off after the factor (20 × 0.5 − 5 = 5). A damage hook that rebuilds damage from `base` folds `ctx.rules` in itself, as it folds `taken` and `guard_mult`.
- **Outgoing** (the credited body's class, `outgoing_damage`, times the session row's) is applied in `resolve` after the hooks, to the health **and** poise damage of a `Hit`, a `Blocked` and a `GuardBroken`. The credit is final there, so it follows a combat object's owner (the object has no class of its own: its hit is ruled by the owner's) and a `credit` a hook names; no hook folds it. A parry, an evade and an ignored hit are not scaled. A factor of 1 is never multiplied in, so a game without rules computes exactly what it computed, and so does a mode that does not name the class **when the session row's outgoing factor for that class is also 1** (an unnamed class still takes the session's factor).
- **Damage that is not a hit.** `deal_damage` is never scaled. `deal_ruled_damage(world, target, amount, credit)` multiplies `amount` by the target's incoming factor and calls it (no outgoing factor: a game that captures a source's power for a later burn multiplies by `shards::rules::outgoing(world, source)` where it captures it).

**Choices where the design is silent (C3.2).** (1) `ActionPlugin` adds `RulesPlugin` when it is missing (design 4.2), so a `shards_action` test app builds without the umbrella; the ordering line `RulesSystems::Apply` before `WorldSystems::Zones` stays the umbrella's (`shards::EnginePlugins`), so an app built by hand with the world's zones adds it itself (`shards_npc`'s test helper does). (2) A block's poise is scaled by the outgoing factor after the guard's `poise_mult`; the incoming factor never touches poise. (3) A hook that names another credit overrides a combat object's owner: the factor follows the final credit.

Tests: `shards_action/tests/combat/rules_damage.rs`.

**Stamina cost (C3.4a).** What starting an action costs is its `cost.stamina` times every `stamina_cost` rule of the body's class that matches it (a rule matches when one of its `tags` is one of the action's `tags` or the action's id; the rules that match multiply): `shards::action::stamina_cost(def, id, rules)`. A mode that has no rule for the action, a body without a class, a game without rules and an action that costs nothing pay `cost.stamina` exactly, so nothing changes for them.

- **Where it counts.** The one start rule every reader shares: the check (`Blocker::Stamina` reports the ruled `need`, and the wait it gives is for that), the start's payment, and a charge's turn, which pays the difference of the two ruled costs. `StaminaMode::Any` keeps its rule: any stamina above 0 starts the action, and it drains to 0 at most. A block's stamina cost (guard damage) is not an action's cost and is not scaled.
- **Every reader sees it.** `FighterView` carries the rules (`rules: Option<RulesView>`), and `FighterView::new` takes them as an argument, so no site that judges a start can leave them out: the action machine; an agent's `Order::Attack` (an order waits for the stamina rather than pressing a swing the machine refuses); a client's prediction (from the replicated `ActiveRules`); the NPC director's grants, the planner's presses, chains and the strike notes (an NPC asks for no attack its stamina cannot pay for); and `FighterView::of`, for the tools.
- **Whose rules.** A body's class is its `RuleClass`, else `player` for a body with a `PlayerId` (`RulesView::of(db, rules, class, player)`, `RulesView::of_entity(world, e)`); an NPC's class is its `RuleClass`.

Tests: `shards_action/tests/combat/rules_costs.rs`, `shards_npc/tests/npc/rules.rs`, `shards_rules` `read.rs` (`a_view_needs_a_set_in_play_and_a_class`).

**Deviations from the design, on purpose.** (1) `RulesPlugin` is in `EnginePlugins` already, with the re-export `shards::rules` and the ordering line `RulesSystems::Apply.before(WorldSystems::Zones)` (the design puts them in C3.1b): the state audit, the engine rule list and the total order of the tick are checked on the whole engine, so the module has to be in it to be tested; `rules` is a module every game runs (it cannot be left out with `--without`). (2) `rules` has no `living` field: `shards_rules` sees neither `Dead` nor the NPC module. (3) The prepare reads `ActiveRules` from the snapshot with serde, as the region's prepare reads its record: the reflected JSON of the resource is the same. (4) `rules_set` refuses without `rules/default`, not only without `ActiveRules`. (5) `cycle` from a mode that is not in `modes` goes to the first (`1`) or the last (`-1`). (6) A content change that takes `rules/default` away leaves a neutral resource; the neutral pass that removes it comes with C3.3a. (7) Rules content that appears in a world without rules in play journals ``rules: content has rules now: the world plays `plain` `` (the design gives no line). (8) A content change treats a neutral resource as an absent one: rules content starts `start` over it. (9) `decides` goes by role (`host` on a host before any peer joins too): the engine's core knows no peer count. (10) On a client the main menu removes its copy of the host's rules (the design sets it neutral): the copy is not the client's to write. (11) The dev entry is `DevCommand::Live` (the design says `Run`), so a game without rules and a client show why it does nothing instead of failing when it runs. (12) `rules_set` refuses a client by itself too, before every other check (the route does it first where a forwarder is set), and a call while a region loads has its own refusal. (13) The `rules` answer has `playing`. (14) A session row must give a column (the design's "each list has 1 to 8 entries": a column left out and an empty one read the same). (15) `start_rules` runs in a public set, `RulesSystems::Start`, for games to order against. (16) A prefab's `RuleClass` that does not read is reported by `rule_class` when there is no type registry, and the "not a class" error lists the classes. (17) The `rules` section sits between `region` and `encounters`, not directly before `position`: the engine registers `encounters` there now (G9), and the mode must be in place before any character section applies, which both orders give. (18) The section's apply calls `shards_rules::load_mode` (the design writes the logic in the section): the role test, the content reads and the event stay inside the rules crate, and a game with its own save section can use it. A mode in a game with no `rules/default` is journalled like any mode the content lacks (``playing no rules``), not skipped silently. (19) `SessionFilter` is `init_resource`d by `RulesPlugin` (it was `insert_resource`d), so the umbrella's filter cannot be overwritten by a plugin order. (20) The engine builds nothing for `--difficulty` (D16 of the design: the game's flag); the manual says how a game does it.
